title: Anesthesia in the Neonate

paragraphs.text: 39 Anesthesia in the Neonate
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: The administration of anesthesia to the neonatal patient requires knowledge and understanding of neonatal anatomy and pathophysiology in addition to the ability to understand how the pharmacology of standard anesthetic drugs is altered in preterm and term neonates. Perioperative surgical anesthetic risk in children increases with decreasing age, making neonatal patients some of the most vulnerable patients anesthesiologists provide anesthetic care for. Anesthesia for these oftentimes critical patients is best performed by specialty-trained pediatric anesthesiologists, as anesthesia-related morbidity is reduced in children anesthetized by pediatric anesthesiologists compared with children cared for by non-pediatric anesthesiologists.1 The American College of Surgeons has developed standards recommending that children under the age of 2 years have anesthesia administered by a pediatric specialty-trained anesthesiologist.2
paragraphs.heading: Safety and Challenges of Neonatal Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: The goals of neonatal anesthesia are similar to those in adults but require different skills, knowledge, and care. The differences between adults and children are most profound in neonates, particularly premature infants. Advances in neonatology and the almost routine survival of infants weighing greater than 1000 g have led to new challenges for pediatric anesthesiologists. Successful anesthetic management in a neonate requires meticulous attention to detail and a thorough understanding of neonatal physiology and development, pharmacology, and pathophysiology. The neonatal period is characterized by immaturity of organ systems, homeostasis, and metabolic pathways. It is a time of major developmental changes, and the effects of anesthesia on that development are not well characterized. Knowledge of the anatomic and physiologic differences among neonates, children, and adults is critical to careful anesthetic administration and management. Maturity of organ systems and metabolic processes varies significantly not only between adults and neonates but also between preterm and term neonates.
paragraphs.heading: Safety and Challenges of Neonatal Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: Personnel, equipment, and the operating room environment need to be specifically adapted for neonates. Monitors, anesthesia delivery systems, mechanical ventilators,
paragraphs.heading: Safety and Challenges of Neonatal Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: and environmental controls all need to be appropriate for use with neonates.
paragraphs.heading: Safety and Challenges of Neonatal Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: It is important to emphasize the perioperative nature of anesthetic management. Anesthesia care does not start and end at the door to the operative suite, and this is as critical in neonates as in older children and adults. Preoperative medical status and current medical management strategies can affect intraoperative care. Transport to the operating room can be one of the most critical aspects of an operation in a premature neonate. The postoperative period requires close monitoring and management of ventilation, fluid balance, and an environment tailored to the special needs of neonates. Assessment and control of postoperative pain require methods and tools specific to neonates.
paragraphs.heading: Safety and Challenges of Neonatal Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: Surgery in neonates is accompanied by a humoral stress response that, left untreated, leads to increased complications and mortality, as shown in the landmark study by Anand and colleagues in 1987.3 This response is diminished by adequate anesthesia (Fig. 39.1, Table 39.1), resulting in improved surgical outcomes. Consequently, over the subsequent decades, adequate anesthesia for all surgical procedures in neonates has been accepted as both a clinical and an ethical imperative.
paragraphs.heading: Safety and Challenges of Neonatal Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: It is also now generally accepted that neonates are capable of sensing pain and discomfort. We have no recallable memories before 3 to 4 years of age (termed infantile amnesia), but neonates do possess consciousness and a sense of self and can form implicit memories—that is, changes in behavior based on prior experience that do not require intentional recall. Plasticity is an inherent characteristic of the developing nervous system, and early pain experiences can lead to exaggerated responses to later painful stimuli or stress, as well as impaired neurodevelopmental outcome.4,5 Activation of brain regions in response to graded moderate pain stimuli is significantly different in school-aged children and adolescents with neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) experience compared with controls, as measured by functional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).6 Based on such evidence, the goals of anesthesia in neonates are not restricted to prevention of the stress response to surgery but also include effective management of pain and discomfort.7,8
paragraphs.heading: Safety and Challenges of Neonatal Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: The safety of modern anesthetics in this vulnerable population continues to be an area of concern, as numerous animal studies have shown neuronal apoptosis and neurocognitive deficits as a result of exposure to virtually all commonly used modern anesthetic agents.9,10 These animal studies, including some in nonhuman primates, have demonstrated abnormal neuroapoptosis and, in some, long-term cognitive deficits, including delayed learning, impaired memory formation and retention, altered motor development, and altered behavioral development. Development of the nervous system is complex, involving neuronal proliferation, migration, differentiation, and “pruning” accomplished by
paragraphs.heading: Safety and Challenges of Neonatal Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: apoptosis. This development is in part dependent on the balance of excitatory and inhibitory stimuli and neurotransmitters. Given the complexity of the process, as well as the obvious physiologic and developmental differences inherent in the application of animal studies to humans, the overall impact of these studies is not completely certain. Concerns have been raised with respect to the animal data regarding dosing and the time course of exposure. A clinically appropriate dose is the minimum necessary to induce anesthesia in the species. In some species, and with some agents, this dose also results in significant mortality, increasing the difficulty of interpreting the significance. Synaptogenesis in rats occurs postnatally over the first 2 weeks of life. An analogous period in humans would range from the third trimester of pregnancy through the first 3 years of life. Whether the child might be susceptible to anesthetic toxicity during this entire period is unknown. Studies in nonhuman primates are assumed to be more translatable to humans. Infant macaques exposed to multiple sevoflurane or isoflurane anesthetics exhibited increased anxiety behaviors and motor reflex deficits.11,12 Finally, most of the animal studies of apoptosis involve anesthesia without surgery. Because neurodevelopment is related to the balance of stimulatory and inhibitory neurotransmitters, there is some indication that the absence of surgical stress may alter the neurodevelopmental response to anesthetics.
paragraphs.heading: Safety and Challenges of Neonatal Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: Prior to 2015, human studies of the long-term effects of anesthetic exposure on the developing brain were largely retrospective and observational, employed varying study designs, and used a wide range of tools to assess neurodevelopmental outcomes. The results were inconsistent and at times conflicting. Exposure to multiple anesthetics during infancy and early childhood was often associated with
paragraphs.heading: Safety and Challenges of Neonatal Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: poorer neurodevelopmental outcomes, whereas a single anesthetic exposure varied between no adverse outcomes to some degree of neurodevelopmental impairment.
paragraphs.heading: Safety and Challenges of Neonatal Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: These concerns led the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), as a result of their ongoing initiative, to study the risk of anesthetic exposure on brain development, to publish a warning in 2016 against repeated or lengthy use of general anesthetics and sedation drugs during surgeries and procedures in children younger than 3 years of age or in pregnant women.13
paragraphs.heading: Safety and Challenges of Neonatal Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: More recent prospective studies with more robust methodology and longer-term follow-up reveal that a single brief anesthetic in early life may have no effect on longterm neurocognitive development. The General Anaesthesia Compared to Spinal Anaesthesia (GAS) study, a prospective randomized controlled trial comparing sevoflurane general anesthesia to awake regional anesthesia (spinal or caudal) for herniorrhaphy in infancy, did not reveal any difference in neurodevelopmental outcome at both 2- and 5-year follow-up.14
paragraphs.heading: Safety and Challenges of Neonatal Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: The Pediatric Anesthesia and Neurodevelopment Assessment (PANDA) study, a prospective sibling-matched cohort study, compared neurocognitive outcomes in infants receiving a short inhaled general anesthetic for herniorrhaphy to a biological sibling with no anesthetic exposure. Follow-up neuropsychological assessment of sibling pairs at ages varying from 8 to 15 years old showed no difference in neurocognitive outcomes.15 The Mayo Anesthesia Safety in Kids (MASK) study, a matched cohort study of almost 1000 children that underwent neuropsychological testing between the ages of 8 and 12 years old or 15 and 19 years old, found that exposure to general anesthesia during childhood was not associated with deficits in cognition.16 In addition, three large retrospective matched cohorts with greater than 59,000 children combined did not find sufficient data to conclude that young age at initial exposure or multiple anesthetic exposures contributed to adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes.17–19
paragraphs.heading: Safety and Challenges of Neonatal Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: No one can question the overwhelming benefit of anesthesia in the setting in which a surgical procedure, or any noxious procedure with significant stress, is required. The detrimental effects of surgical stress have been well shown. Similarly, the benefits of early repair of some surgical problems, such as congenital heart defects or neonatal hernia with risk of incarceration, have been shown, although such repair may lead to anesthesia at a younger, and potentially more susceptible, age. When deciding to proceed with an anesthetic, the benefit versus the risk of delay in surgical procedures, particularly if performed in premature infants, should be carefully considered. Reassuringly, current human studies suggest that a short anesthetic exposure during early development is safe.
paragraphs.heading: Safety and Challenges of Neonatal Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: The presence of certain comorbidities along with intrinsic surgical risk play a role in estimating perioperative risk of

paragraphs.text: morbidity and mortality for all pediatric patients. A retrospective multivariate analysis of over 350,000 surgical cases determined that the presence of the following risk factors in the setting of higher risk surgical procedures was associated with risk for 30-day mortality:20 • Weight <5 kg • American Society of Anesthesiology (ASA) status III or
paragraphs.heading: Preoperative Evaluation and Preparation

paragraphs.text: higher • Preoperative sepsis • Inotropic support • Ventilator dependence prior to surgery
paragraphs.heading: Preoperative Evaluation and Preparation

paragraphs.text: Similar findings were found in the Neonate-Children Study of Anaesthesia Practice in Europe (NECTARINE) study.21 These comorbidities are present in many neonatal patients along with the need for some higher-risk surgical procedures. Understanding the risks undertaken with both the anesthetic and the surgical procedure for a given patient allows for an informed discussion with both families and the neonatology team.
paragraphs.heading: Preoperative Evaluation and Preparation

paragraphs.text: The preoperative evaluation should include the neonate’s current physical condition, including significant illness, the degree of transition from fetal to newborn physiology, maturity, and the presence of any congenital anomalies. Particular attention should be paid to cardiorespiratory status, required ventilatory or hemodynamic support, blood chemistries, and nutritional support.
paragraphs.heading: Preoperative Evaluation and Preparation

paragraphs.text: A full maternal history including the course of pregnancy, labor, and delivery provides important details. A family history of anesthetic difficulties, most importantly a history of malignant hyperthermia or pseudocholinesterase deficiency, must be obtained as these conditions alter the choice of medications that can be used to perform a safe anesthetic. Maternal diseases such as diabetes, systemic lupus erythematosus, and preeclampsia have implications for the neonate. Congenital infections, oligohydramnios, intrauterine growth restriction, and maternal drug and alcohol use are also important considerations.
paragraphs.heading: Preoperative Evaluation and Preparation

paragraphs.text: Gestational age, birth weight, and postnatal age affect anesthetic care. Birth weight does not accurately reflect maturity unless the infant is appropriate for gestational age, which is defined as being within 2 standard deviations of the mean for gestational age. Infants who are small for gestational age are more mature than their birth weight would indicate. Infants who are large for gestational age are often children of diabetic mothers, and they are at increased risk of hypoglycemia in the first 48 hours after birth. A history of birth asphyxia or neonatal resuscitation and Apgar scores can provide information about the health status of the neonate.
paragraphs.heading: Preoperative Evaluation and Preparation

paragraphs.text: Medical history should include complete details of the present illness and treatment. Medications and administration times, details of vascular access, and respiratory parameters including ventilator type and settings all are crucial details, especially in sicker infants. Infants on highfrequency oscillatory ventilation may need to be switched to conventional ventilation and observed for several hours to facilitate movement to an operating room. If the infant
paragraphs.heading: Preoperative Evaluation and Preparation

paragraphs.text: is on some other modality, such as inhaled nitric oxide or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, arrangements may also need to be made, and transport to the operating room would require more resources and assistance.
paragraphs.heading: Preoperative Evaluation and Preparation

paragraphs.text: The time of the last oral feed should be noted to assure that appropriate nil per os (NPO, nothing by mouth) guidelines have been met. Attenuation of airway reflexes with induction of anesthesia places the infant at risk for aspiration of acidic gastric contents, which can lead to serious inflammatory pneumonitis. These guidelines are summarized in Table 39.222 and are meant to ensure that the volume and composition of gastric contents are as minimal as possible. However, attempts should be made to avoid longer than necessary NPO times to prevent interruptions in vital nutrition and avoid dehydration. The intake of clear fluids up to 2 hours prior to the induction of anesthesia is actually encouraged, as it can help to avoid fluctuations in blood glucose levels, avoids neonatal distress due to hunger, and improves parental satisfaction. In neonates, dehydration and hypoglycemia occur much more quickly than in older patients, and this risk is even greater in an infant without an intravenous line if NPO times are prolonged.
paragraphs.heading: Preoperative Evaluation and Preparation

paragraphs.text: Gastric emptying is delayed with stress, anxiety, and illness. Infants with diseases such as pyloric stenosis, duodenal atresia, malrotation, or other obstructive lesions are often already NPO leading up to surgery, and they need an intravenous line to maintain appropriate hydration. Despite the NPO status, there usually are significant gastric contents, and rapid-sequence induction and intubation are required if there is any concern for obstruction. Emptying the stomach via nasogastric drainage is undependable and usually inadequate. Gastric feeds even in intubated infants also should be discontinued at an appropriate time because the infant may need to be reintubated during surgery, and a full stomach would increase the risk for aspiration.
paragraphs.heading: Preoperative Evaluation and Preparation

paragraphs.text: Physical examination should include an assessment of vital signs noting trends or recent changes. Careful attention should be paid to evaluation of the cardiorespiratory system. Many neonates requiring surgery are ill and are at risk for hemodynamic or respiratory instability.
paragraphs.heading: Preoperative Evaluation and Preparation

paragraphs.text: The presence of any congenital anomalies must be noted, as they may have an impact on anesthetic care. Often, a group of defects suggests a well-recognized and characterized syndrome. A number of common syndromes with their anesthetic implications are listed in Table 39.3.
paragraphs.heading: Preoperative Evaluation and Preparation

paragraphs.text: Difficult intubation is a common problem in infants with congenital defects, and the airway must be carefully assessed. The presence of micrognathia or retrognathia can be an indicator of a difficult airway. Intraoral, facial or neck masses may make a neonate difficult to both mask ventilate and intubate. Limitations in neck mobility can also affect airway management. Because of the tendency for rapid oxygen desaturation in infants, difficulties with intubation can be extremely serious. In infants who are already intubated, tube size and position should be evaluated. The pressure at which a leak occurs around the tube should be documented. The quantity and consistency of secretions and need for
paragraphs.heading: Preoperative Evaluation and Preparation

paragraphs.text: frequent suctioning should be ascertained. The small tubes required in premature infants can easily be blocked by tenacious secretions and are easily dislodged. If there is any question about adequacy of intubation, the infant should be electively reintubated before surgery; emergently replacing an endotracheal tube under the drapes after beginning an operation is not a benign procedure.
paragraphs.heading: Preoperative Evaluation and Preparation

paragraphs.text: Preoperative evaluation of the pulmonary system in the neonate should include a review of recent chest x-rays, notation of current ventilation or oxygen therapies (including ventilator settings), and a physical exam noting work of breathing, stridor, or adventitious lung sounds. History related to length of intubation, prior modes of ventilation, and current issues related to apneas, desaturations, and bradycardia should be obtained. The pulmonary circulation in a neonate is hyperreactive; multiple stressors including surgical stimulation can initiate episodes of pulmonary hypertension, resulting in decreased cardiac output and oxygen desaturation. Any history of such spells requires increased vigilance to avoid hypoxia, hypercarbia, and acidosis, which increase pulmonary resistance. Infants with bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) are at risk of pulmonary hypertension and susceptible to excessive pulmonary vasoconstriction in response to hypoxia, hypothermia, or acidosis. Because of their chronic lung disease, these infants may have some degree of right heart dysfunction, and decreases in myocardial function related to anesthetics may result in acute right heart failure. Patients with severe BPD may benefit from an echocardiogram to evaluate for evidence of pulmonary hypertension prior to undergoing anesthesia. Other problems in BPD include airway hyperreactivity, increased airway secretions, electrolyte abnormalities because of diuretic therapy, and frequently tracheomalacia.23
paragraphs.heading: Preoperative Evaluation and Preparation

paragraphs.text: Evaluation of cardiac status should investigate for congenital heart disease, as well as identify patients who might be at higher risk of intraoperative hemodynamic instability due to the need for preoperative inotropic support. Major congenital anomalies requiring operative intervention within the first days to weeks of life, including omphalocele, congenital diaphragmatic hernia, tracheoesophageal fistula, duodenal atresia, and imperforate anus, are often more highly associated with congenital heart disease.24 Echocardiograms are frequently performed for these patients prior to surgery and anesthesia.
