paragraphs.text: carefully assessed because major shifts can occur easily during surgery. One of the most common left-to-right shunts is a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). The infant should be carefully evaluated for signs of congestive heart failure, such as hepatic congestion, enlarged heart, and edema. The presence of single ventricle physiology is particularly important because the anesthesiologist needs to take great care to maintain balance between the pulmonary and systemic circulations. High inspired oxygen concentration in these infants results in pulmonary vasodilation and pulmonary overcirculation at the expense of systemic circulation, with consequent acidosis. Particular attention should be paid to ventilation; in some cases, increased carbon dioxide (CO2) concentrations may be beneficial as a way to limit pulmonary blood flow in patients with large left-to-right shunts. Abnormal pulses on physical examination may indicate coarctation of the aorta. Antibiotic prophylaxis for
paragraphs.heading: Anesthetic Implications of Neonatal Syndromes—cont’d

paragraphs.text: endocarditis is also often important in neonates with congenital heart disease. Intrinsic arrhythmias are unusual in a neonate, although congenital heart block may occur in infants of mothers with systemic lupus erythematosus.
paragraphs.heading: Anesthetic Implications of Neonatal Syndromes—cont’d

paragraphs.text: Neurologic function should be carefully assessed. Hemodynamic changes during surgery may affect cerebral blood flow. A history of seizures should increase the anesthesiologist’s level of suspicion for intraoperative seizure if there is unexplained tachycardia or blood pressure elevations. The presence of intraventricular hemorrhage requires increased care to maintain hemodynamic stability and is a contraindication to procedures requiring anticoagulation. A history of hydrocephalus mandates avoidance of factors that increase intracranial pressure.
paragraphs.heading: Anesthetic Implications of Neonatal Syndromes—cont’d

paragraphs.text: Laboratory studies need to be reviewed, if applicable. Hemoglobin levels should be greater than 10 g/dL to ensure adequate oxygen delivery to the tissues, given the
paragraphs.heading: Anesthetic Implications of Neonatal Syndromes—cont’d

paragraphs.text: decreased unloading at the tissue level by fetal hemoglobin. Metabolic acidosis should be corrected, preferably by reversal of the cause of the acidosis. Electrolyte levels help to guide fluid management; hypocalcemia should be corrected. For most operations, it is important to check that blood for transfusion is available; for major procedures, fresh frozen plasma and platelets for transfusion also may be required.
paragraphs.heading: Anesthetic Implications of Neonatal Syndromes—cont’d

paragraphs.text: In utero, the pulmonary circulation is a high-resistance circuit so that the lungs receive little blood flow, and oxygenation is a placental function. At birth, amniotic fluid is expelled from the lungs, the lungs expand, and respiration begins. The lungs are initially very stiff (compliance very low), and the first breath may require negative forces of 70 cm H2O or more. Pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) decreases rapidly with lung distention, while oxygenation, pulmonary blood flow, and cardiac output increase. The increase in pulmonary blood flow coupled with decreased venous return from the inferior vena cava with clamping of the placenta causes left atrial pressure to exceed right atrial pressure, resulting in closure of the foramen ovale. The ductus arteriosus should functionally close between 1 and 15 hours after birth.
paragraphs.heading: Transition Phase and Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Neonate

paragraphs.text: Although PVR decreases, the pulmonary arterioles possess abundant smooth muscle, and the pulmonary vascular bed remains very reactive. In this setting, hypoxia, hypercarbia, or acidosis can cause a sudden increase in PVR and a return to a fetal circulatory pattern, a condition known as persistent fetal circulation or persistent pulmonary hypertension of the neonate (PPHN). PPHN is an acute, life-threatening condition, as shunt fraction increases to 70% to 80%, and profound cyanosis results. Many factors during anesthesia can affect this transitional state. Anesthetic agents can markedly diminish systemic vascular resistance (SVR), resulting in a right-to-left shunt. Hypoxia or hypercarbia and acidosis from inadequate ventilation can increase PVR. Surgical stimulation and the surgical stress response can cause sympathetic stimulation and a release of catechols that can cause abrupt increases in PVR. Anesthetic care of a neonate, especially in the first few days of life, needs to take into account the reactivity of the pulmonary vascular bed. Pulse oximetry should be monitored in both a pre- and postductal location in order to allow for early identification of PDA shunt reversal if PVR increases. Adequate anesthesia and analgesia must be maintained to prevent excessive catecholamine release. When caring for neonates with known or high risk for pulmonary hypertension, pulmonary vasodilators such as inhaled nitric oxide and options for inotropic support should be immediately available.
paragraphs.heading: Transition Phase and Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Neonate

paragraphs.text: Compared with older children and adults, in neonates lung volume and functional residual capacity (FRC) as a percentage of body size are much less. Alveolar ventilation per unit lung volume is very high, because the neonate’s metabolic rate is about twice that of an adult. Most of this alveolar ventilation is provided by a rapid respiratory rate of 35 to 40 breaths/min because tidal volume is limited due to the structure of the chest wall.
paragraphs.heading: Respiratory Mechanics, Central Control of Ventilation, and Apnea

paragraphs.text: One consequence of the reduced FRC and high metabolic rate in a neonate is a diminished reserve. Changes in the fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2) are rapidly seen as changes in the partial pressure of oxygen (PaO2), and the neonate quickly desaturates if ventilation is interrupted. This situation limits time for intubation, and airway management can be challenging. The high alveolar ventilation also accounts for a very rapid uptake of inhalational anesthetic agents, especially in premature infants, making it easy to overdose with these agents. Closing volume, which is the lung volume at which smaller airways tend to collapse, is very close to FRC in neonates. It is well known that anesthesia causes decreases in FRC. In a neonate, this low closing volume can result in airway closure at end expiration, with resultant atelectasis, ventilation/perfusion mismatch, and increased intrapulmonary shunting.
paragraphs.heading: Respiratory Mechanics, Central Control of Ventilation, and Apnea

paragraphs.text: An awake infant uses laryngeal braking, resulting in an auto-positive end-expiratory pressure (auto-PEEP) to maintain FRC, but laryngeal braking is diminished by anesthesia. In a premature neonate, alveoli are immature, thick walled, and saccular. Surfactant production begins at 23 to 24 weeks’ gestation, but it may remain inadequate until 36 weeks’ gestational age; because of this, lung volumes and compliance are decreased further in very premature infants. Although the lung is less compliant in an infant than in an older child, the chest wall in an infant is very compliant. This combination results in increased work of breathing. Because resistance to airflow is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the radius of the airway, the work of breathing is increased further in neonates, particularly small premature infants.
paragraphs.heading: Respiratory Mechanics, Central Control of Ventilation, and Apnea

paragraphs.text: Changes in airway resistance are also common during anesthesia, often resulting from small endotracheal tubes and equipment factors such as inspiratory and expiratory valves in the breathing circuit. Kinking of the endotracheal tube or the presence of secretions also can adversely affect resistance. Respiratory failure from fatigue can occur easily. Most anesthetic agents are respiratory depressants. Central regulation of breathing is obtunded under anesthesia, with a significant decrease in the ventilatory response to increased CO2. Most neonates require controlled positive-pressure ventilation during operative procedures because of the low FRC, increased closing volume, and increased work, along with changes induced by anesthetics. Infants already being ventilated require some increase in their ventilator settings after induction of anesthesia as spontaneous respiratory
paragraphs.heading: Respiratory Mechanics, Central Control of Ventilation, and Apnea

paragraphs.text: drive is abolished, and some infants require increased postoperative ventilatory support due to anesthesia-induced atelectasis, sedation, or changes in pulmonary function as a result of the surgery itself.
paragraphs.heading: Respiratory Mechanics, Central Control of Ventilation, and Apnea

paragraphs.text: Tracheomalacia is common in premature infants and, if low in the airway, may not be obviated by intubation. Bronchomalacia may result in airway collapse on expiration. Laryngomalacia is also common in premature infants and can result in obstruction with sedation prior to securing the airway. Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) or PEEP increases FRC and decreases closing volume and helps to stent open the airway during anesthesia. Slower respiratory rates should be used with positive-pressure ventilation to allow time for passive exhalation and prevent air trapping. Pneumothorax and interstitial emphysema may develop if high peak inspiratory pressures are used. Careful attention must be paid to ventilator settings, and one should anticipate changes that may need to occur during a surgical procedure.
paragraphs.heading: Respiratory Mechanics, Central Control of Ventilation, and Apnea

paragraphs.text: Periodic breathing with intermittent apneic spells is common in neonates up to 3 months of age. Small premature infants have a biphasic ventilatory response to hypoxia, with an initial increase in ventilation, followed by a progressive decrease and eventual apnea. The ventilatory response to CO2 is decreased in premature infants and, as noted, is decreased further by anesthesia. Postoperative apneic spells are common in premature infants, although incidence decreases with advancing postconceptional age (PCA). These episodes can be secondary to the immature respiratory control system (central), a floppy airway (obstructive), or both (mixed or combined). Cote and coworkers25 did a meta-analysis of data from eight separate studies, and it was clear that the risk of apnea was strongly inversely related to gestational age and PCA. A full-term neonate is unlikely to experience significant postoperative apnea after 45 weeks’ PCA, whereas an infant born prematurely is at risk for postoperative apnea until 55 to 60 weeks’ PCA.25 The risk of postoperative apnea is increased in neonates who are anemic, suffer from neurologic disease, or are still currently experiencing apneic episodes. It is for these reasons that neonates coming in from home for surgical procedures are kept for a 12- to 24-hour period of respiratory monitoring until they are greater than 45 weeks’ PCA (full-term infants) or 55 to 60 weeks’ PCA (preterm infants).
paragraphs.heading: Respiratory Mechanics, Central Control of Ventilation, and Apnea

paragraphs.text: BPD is one of the most common complications of prematurity and can range from mild oxygen requirement to severe forms requiring prolonged mechanical ventilation with the development of pulmonary hypertension. The risk of BPD increases with decreasing gestational age at birth, as well as a number of other risk factors present at or shortly after birth.
paragraphs.heading: Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia and Oxygen Therapy

paragraphs.text: Mechanical ventilation increases the risk of damage to the alveoli; however, mechanical ventilation is almost always
paragraphs.heading: Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia and Oxygen Therapy

paragraphs.text: necessary intraoperatively with neonates. Especially in patients with severe BPD, low lung compliance at baseline makes invasive ventilation necessary in order to adequately oxygenate and ventilate while under the influence of anesthetic drugs as well as the potential need for muscle relaxation. In an attempt to avoid volutrauma and barotrauma, smaller tidal volumes should be employed with tolerance for mild hypercapnia (partial pressure of carbon dioxide in arterial blood [PaCO2], 55–60 mm Hg) assuming that pH is normal.23 Careful attention should be paid to the volume of intravenous fluids administered to avoid fluid overload and pulmonary edema, which can cause further lung damage.
paragraphs.heading: Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia and Oxygen Therapy

paragraphs.text: Oxygen is a highly reactive molecule, and free-radical formation by oxygen is well known. Reperfusion injury, which refers to damage resulting from free-radical formation on oxygenation after a period of hypoxia, is well established. Retinopathy of prematurity is the most widely known complication of hyperoxia, but there is increasing evidence that oxygen may play a role in chronic lung disease, neurologic impairment, and other pathologic conditions. There is also evidence that wide fluctuations in oxygenation, as often experienced during anesthesia, may be damaging.
paragraphs.heading: Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia and Oxygen Therapy

paragraphs.text: Monitoring of oxygenation during operative procedures is problematic. Continuous pulse oximetry is the standard of care and has contributed to the safety of anesthesia by avoidance of hypoxia. The pulse oximeter is not as helpful for the detection of hyperoxia. At hemoglobin saturations greater than 95%, most infants are hyperoxic; this is altered further by varying amounts of fetal hemoglobin. It has been suggested that for ongoing management of neonates in the NICU, oxygen saturation targets of 90% to 95% should be used.26 During the induction of anesthesia, brief increases in FiO2 are often necessary to allow for greater oxygen reserve while apneic during intubation; however, oxygen concentrations should be decreased quickly after the airway is secured. The presence of experienced personnel during intubation reduces the risk of prolonged apnea and desaturation during intubation. Intraoperatively, higher than normal oxygen concentrations may become necessary at times due to surgical techniques that may affect gas exchange (lung retraction, insufflation during laparoscopy, lateral decubitus positioning). Care must be taken to be cognizant of inspired oxygen concentrations, keeping them at the lowest concentration to maintain appropriate saturations whenever possible. Current anesthesia practice involves minimizing excessive oxygen administration in preterm neonates as long as oxygen saturation is 90% or greater.
paragraphs.heading: Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia and Oxygen Therapy

paragraphs.text: Airway anatomy in neonates and infants differs from that of older children and must be taken into consideration when airway management is anticipated. The infant’s head is much larger relative to its body size, with a more prominent occiput and shorter neck than those of older children. The infant’s tongue is large, but the larynx is higher and anterior, with the cords located at C4 in the infant
paragraphs.heading: Airway Anatomy

paragraphs.text: compared with C5 or C6 in an adult. The epiglottis of the infant is soft and folded. The neonate’s larynx has historically been described as conical, with the narrowest point in the subglottic area at the cricoid ring. Studies have revisited this anatomy using MRI27 and video-bronchoscopic imaging.28 Based on these studies, the larynx is cylindrical, although not round in cross-section but rather elliptical, with the anteroposterior dimension slightly greater. A tight-fitting, round endotracheal tube might compress the lateral laryngeal mucosa; subglottic stenosis remains a concern, especially with longer term intubation. Current practice in pediatric anesthesia utilizes cuffed endotracheal tubes for most pediatric patients when intubating for surgical procedures.29 Changes in respiratory mechanics can occur as a result of surgical technique (laparoscopy, thoracoscopy, large abdominal incision with retraction). A cuffed endotracheal tube allows for changes in tidal volumes or inspiratory pressures with fewer leaks as lung compliance changes throughout the case.30 The endotracheal tube also protects the airway from aspiration of gastric contents or blood present due to surgical manipulation. There are robust safety data regarding the use of cuffed endotracheal tubes, even long term, in patients greater than 3 kg. Newer tubes with thin, low-pressure cuffs have allowed for the safe use of cuffed endotracheal tubes. Microcuff tubes are available with very thin cuffs and without the Murphy eye, which decreases the length of the tube below the cuff. This ensures that the entirety of the cuff is below the cords, avoiding pressure on the cords. A cuffed tube can be sized smaller, because the cuff prevents leakage and could decrease the incidence of subglottic stenosis rather than increase it, as previously believed, especially when attention is paid to cuff pressures. For patients less than 3 kg, little to no data are available regarding the use of cuffed endotracheal tubes as cuffed endotracheal tubes are only available down to 3.0-mm internal diameter.
paragraphs.heading: Airway Anatomy

paragraphs.text: Laryngeal and tracheal trauma is important because even modest airway edema can be serious. At the cricoid ring, 1 mm of edema results in a 60% reduction in the cross-sectional area of the airway, causing increased airway resistance and increased work of breathing.
paragraphs.heading: Airway Anatomy

paragraphs.text: Immediately after birth, with an open ductus arteriosus, most of the cardiac output is from the left ventricle, and left ventricular end-diastolic volume is very high. Consequently, the neonatal heart functions at the high end of the Starling curve. As PVR decreases, output from the two ventricles becomes balanced at 150 to 200 mL/kg/min. Heart rate is rapid at 130 to 160 beats/min. Because end-diastolic volumes are already high, the infant heart is unable to increase stroke volume to a significant degree, and increases in cardiac output depend entirely on increases in heart rate. Baseline blood pressure is lower in infants than in older children, particularly in preterm infants, because cardiac output is increased due to a low SVR.
paragraphs.heading: Cardiac Physiology

paragraphs.text: Almost all anesthetic agents have significant effects on the cardiovascular system. Inhalational agents tend to be cardiovascular depressants, and they can result in decreased myocardial contractility and subsequent decreased cardiac output. Most anesthetic agents cause decreased autonomic tone and peripheral vasodilation, decreasing afterload and preload. Because baroreceptor reflexes also are blunted by anesthesia, these decreases may make it impossible for the infant to compensate for pre-existing volume contraction or volume losses during anesthesia. Inotropic support may be necessary in a sick neonate, and almost all infants require some degree of volume loading during anesthesia to support tissue perfusion, urine output, and metabolic needs in the setting of anesthetic effects on hemodynamics.
paragraphs.heading: Cardiac Physiology

paragraphs.text: The infant has approximately 80% fetal hemoglobin (hemoglobin F) at birth. Hemoglobin F has a P50 (PaO2 at which hemoglobin is 50% saturated) of 20 mm Hg compared with a P50 of 27 mm Hg for hemoglobin A, which means that hemoglobin F has a higher affinity for oxygen and that the hemoglobin dissociation curve is shifted to the left. In utero, this hemoglobin dissociation curve favors transport of oxygen from the maternal to the fetal circulation. Put another way, for any given oxygen saturation, the infant has a lower PaO2. Unloading of oxygen at the tissue level also is diminished, although this is compensated for by an increased hemoglobin level of approximately 17.5 g/dL at birth. The decreased unloading can result in tissue hypoxia, however, if PaO2, hemoglobin, or cardiac output decreases during surgery, with secondary development of metabolic acidosis. The hemoglobin increases slightly just after birth, then decreases progressively to a level of 9.5 to 11 g/dL by 7 to 9 weeks of life due to reduced red blood cell life span, increasing blood volume, and immature hematopoiesis. Hemoglobin F synthesis begins to decrease after 35 weeks’ gestation, and hemoglobin F is completely replaced by hemoglobin A by 8 to 12 weeks of life, paralleling the decrease in hemoglobin and helping to maintain tissue oxygenation. The physiologic hemoglobin nadir may occur earlier and may be more pronounced in premature infants, as they have impaired erythropoietin production as well as potential blood losses from frequent phlebotomy and reduced red blood cell life span. These factors place them at higher risk for anemia of prematurity. Preoperative anemia in neonates has been found to be an independent risk factor for mortality after noncardiac surgery.31 When these patients present for surgical procedures requiring anesthesia, an otherwise well-tolerated physiologic anemia may necessitate transfusion in the operating room to optimize tissue oxygenation, replacing even small amounts of blood loss. Anemia is also a risk factor for postoperative apnea, which may have an effect on the ability to successfully extubate a premature neonate after an anesthetic. It is for these reasons that preoperative red blood cell transfusions with a hemoblobin goal of at least 10 g/dL is indicated in anemic neonates.
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Hemoglobin and Anemia

paragraphs.text: Nephrogenesis is complete at 34 weeks’ gestation, and the term neonate has as many nephrons as an adult, although they are immature, with a glomerular filtration rate (GFR) approximately 30% of the adult GFR. With increasing cardiac output and decreasing renal vascular resistance, renal blood flow and GFR increase rapidly over the first few weeks of life and reach adult levels by about 1 year of life. The diminished function over the first year is well balanced to the infant’s needs, because much of the neonate’s solute load is incorporated into body growth, and the excretory load is smaller.
paragraphs.heading: Renal Physiology

paragraphs.text: Several aspects of renal physiology are pertinent to anesthesia care. First, the neonatal kidney has only limited concentrating ability, whereas antidiuretic hormone secretion and activity are normal. Coupled with an increased insensible loss due to a “thin” skin and increased ratio of surface area to volume, the limited concentrating ability of the kidney implies a tendency to become water depleted if intake or administration is inadequate. The neonatal kidney also is unable to excrete dilute urine efficiently and cannot handle a large free water load. In addition, primarily due to a short, immature proximal tubule, infants are obligate sodium wasters. There is a tendency toward hyponatremia, especially if too much free water is administered during surgery, which can easily happen with continuous infusions from invasive pressure transducers or fluid boluses. Because of the lower GFR, the neonate also cannot handle a large sodium load and can easily develop volume overload and congestive heart failure. With the frequent need for volume or blood product administration in the operative setting, consideration of immature renal physiology must occur.
paragraphs.heading: Renal Physiology

paragraphs.text: One final aspect of concern is acid-base status: The neonatal kidney wastes small amounts of bicarbonate due to an immature proximal tubule; infants are born with a mild proximal renal tubular acidosis, with serum bicarbonate of approximately 20 mmol/L. All of these changes are greater in preterm infants, particularly before nephrogenesis is complete at 34 weeks.
paragraphs.heading: Renal Physiology

paragraphs.text: Given a large surface area, small body volume, and minimal insulation, neonates are extremely prone to heat loss. Any degree of cold stress is detrimental and increases metabolic demands in the neonate. Infants are unable to shiver effectively, and cold stress causes catecholamine release, which stimulates nonshivering thermogenesis by brown fat. Premature infants have less brown fat, decreasing their capacity for nonshivering thermogenesis and increasing their risk for hypothermia. The increased catechols caused by cold stress can be detrimental, causing increased peripheral vascular resistance and SVR, increased cardiac stress, and increased oxygen consumption. Anesthesia blunts thermoregulatory sensitivity and interferes with nonshivering thermogenesis and brown fat metabolism. Anesthesia also increases heat loss
paragraphs.heading: Temperature Regulation

paragraphs.text: by inducing cutaneous vasodilation. Surgical factors such as major operations with open body cavities also contribute to increased risks of hypothermia in the neonate. Hypothermia can result in increased metabolic oxygen demand, respiratory depression, bradycardia, coagulopathy, and impaired wound healing. At all times, including during transport and in the operating room, the infant must be subjected to a neutral thermal environment. An environment that is too warm can be equally detrimental. Core temperature must be carefully monitored at all times in the operating room. Higher than normal ambient operating room temperatures, forced air warmers, overhead radiant warmers, warming of fluids and blood products prior to administration, and minimizing exposure (such as wearing hats) are methods to help maintain euthermia during surgery.
paragraphs.heading: Temperature Regulation

paragraphs.text: Whole-body glucose demand corrected for body mass in neonates can be twice that in adults. Carbohydrate reserves, primarily hepatic glycogen, in a normal newborn are relatively low, and even lower in an infant with low birth weight. Hypoglycemia can readily occur if the infant is deprived of a glucose source. Under anesthesia, the symptoms of hypoglycemia (jitteriness, altered level of consciousness, apnea, tachypnea, poor feeding) are masked, so careful monitoring of serum glucose is indicated for procedures lasting longer than 2 to 3 hours so that low serum glucose levels are not missed. Even transient hypoglycemia may be associated with neurologic injury and developmental delay in neonates.32 Generally, intravenous glucose or intravenous hyperalimentation should be continued during periods of preoperative fasting and intraoperatively, especially in infants with low birth weight without adequate glycogen or fat stores. In contrast with adults in whom hyperglycemia seems to potentiate brain damage during global and focal ischemia, hyperglycemia in neonates may provide some protection from ischemic damage.58 Nonetheless, hyperglycemia can also be a problem in the perioperative period. Insulin response is deficient in preterm infants, and high catecholamines due to illness or intraoperative stress can result in hyperglycemia.
paragraphs.heading: Carbohydrate Metabolism

paragraphs.text: Transport of a premature infant may be as great a risk as the surgery itself. Dedicated transport incubators, with a built-in ventilator, air and oxygen supplies, and a blender should be used if possible. In addition to the inherent risks involved in the transport of a potentially unstable patient, premature neonates are particularly susceptible to cold stress. Heat loss during transport must be addressed because the hospital corridors are rarely neutral thermal environments. If the infant is in an incubator, the incubator should be used for transport, because heat is retained even when it is unplugged. An infant on an open radiant warmer should be covered, including the head. In some institutions, plastic
paragraphs.heading: Transport of the Neonate

paragraphs.text: wrap is used to retain heat and reduce evaporative losses. Disposable chemical warmer packs are available and can be used under the infant either in an incubator or on the radiant warmer.
paragraphs.heading: Transport of the Neonate

paragraphs.text: A need for assisted ventilation presents additional problems. During hand bagging with an anesthesia bag, CPAP or PEEP is generally lost. The use of a simple oxygen tank limits ventilation to 100% FiO2, so controlled oxygen delivery requires an additional air tank and a blender. The anesthesia bag always should include a manometer, because it is easy to reach pressures that can result in barotrauma complications such as pneumothorax. A self-inflating resuscitator can be used for room-air ventilation, and a PEEP valve can be added to the device. In an intubated infant, CPAP or PEEP can be maintained using devices such as the Neopuff. Particular care must be taken not to dislodge the endotracheal tube; small changes can result in either extubation or endobronchial intubation, particularly in a very premature infant. A laryngoscope, endotracheal tubes, and a face mask should be taken on transport in case the endotracheal tube is dislodged.
paragraphs.heading: Transport of the Neonate

paragraphs.text: It is not uncommon for even extremely premature infants to be managed with noninvasive ventilator assistance such as nasal continuous positive airway pressure (NCPAP) or nasal intermittent positive-pressure ventilation (NIPPV), which has reduced the rates of mechanical ventilation and the risk of BPD.33 These types of noninvasive ventilation require special equipment that is not always portable for transport. Plans for transport of neonates on these modes of noninvasive ventilation must include a discussion of the respiratory support with which the patient can be transported. Unfortunately, these modes of ventilation do not easily translate into usage in the operating room, and most of these neonates will still require intubation for controlled positive-pressure ventilation during their surgical procedure.
paragraphs.heading: Transport of the Neonate

paragraphs.text: For all but the healthiest neonates, a physician experienced in neonatal resuscitation and who has the ability to manage critically ill neonates should accompany the transport. In most situations, this person should be the anesthesiologist. Monitoring during transport varies depending on the condition of the infant. As a minimum, a pulse oximeter provides pulse rate and arterial oxygen saturation. In most ill neonates, an electrocardiogram (ECG) and blood pressure should also be monitored, especially if the infant has an indwelling arterial line. Any pumps providing infusions to the infant should have adequate battery power to operate throughout the transport, especially if vasoactive drips are running. Syringe pumps provide a very stable rate and have a long battery life, and the entire system is compact, minimizing the equipment needing transport. These pumps also run accurately at a low (0.5 mL/h) rate so that concentrated infusions can be used, minimizing fluid delivered to the neonate.
paragraphs.heading: Transport of the Neonate

paragraphs.text: A complete round of resuscitative medications also should accompany any infant being transported to or from the NICU. Transports often require multiple personnel— anesthesia staff, nursing, and respiratory therapy. With
paragraphs.heading: Transport of the Neonate

paragraphs.text: planning and adequate personnel, the transport of infants on extracorporeal membrane oxygenation or infants receiving inhaled nitric oxide is possible.
paragraphs.heading: Transport of the Neonate

paragraphs.text: In some situations, if the surgical procedure is appropriate, the surgeon is amenable, and a suitable location is available, it may be preferable to perform some procedures in the NICU. Basic requirements for a suitable locale include a clean area that can be closed off from traffic and adequate equipment, including overhead lights, surgical instruments and supplies, appropriate monitors, and anesthesia equipment. For premature neonates, an anesthesia machine is not usually needed, and a standard neonatal ventilator can be used. In many state-of-the-art NICUs, there is a dedicated operating room, with appropriate equipment, gases, and lights within the NICU, so that the most critically ill infants can be cared for with minimal transport.
paragraphs.heading: Transport of the Neonate

paragraphs.text: The operating room should not merely replicate NICU capabilities; it should surpass them, because the neonate is subjected to the additional stress and destabilization of surgery. It is helpful if the room itself has adequate temperature control, because it may be necessary to increase room temperature to obtain a neutral thermal environment. Before draping, radiant heat lamps can be used, although care must be taken not to place the lamps too close to the infant because overheating can occur. The operating tables for neonates should use a heating pad. For longer cases, forcedair heaters with a “full access” disposable air blanket that is placed under the infant may be used. Care does have to be taken that the sheets and drapes around the infant are dry, however, as evaporative cooling can occur with the continuous air flow if the child is wet. Maintenance fluids, because they are given at a relatively slow rate, usually can be given at room temperature, but fluid warmers must be available for blood or faster fluid administration. Cooling is rarely necessary, but it is possible to overheat an infant if care is not taken. Temperature must be monitored. Core temperature should be measured whenever possible. It can be measured with a rectal, nasopharyngeal, or esophageal probe. Bladder and tympanic membrane probes are rarely used in neonates because of size. Skin temperature is a poor choice for monitoring temperature, as it often better approximates the environmental temperature rather than the core temperature in a small infant.
paragraphs.heading: Operating Room Equipment and Monitoring

paragraphs.text: Routine monitoring requirements for neonates are listed in Box 39.1. Continuous pulse oximetry has revolutionized anesthesia, and it is a standard of care in neonates as in adults. In some situations, particularly with congenital heart disease or PPHN, two pulse oximeters may be used to monitor preductal and postductal oxygen saturations. Heart rate is monitored from the pulse oximeter and the ECG. Disposable neonatal ECG pads are needed, from a size standard and because they may adhere better to the vernix-covered skin of the neonate. Noninvasive blood pressure can be measured, and most available machines have neonatal cuffs
paragraphs.heading: Operating Room Equipment and Monitoring

paragraphs.text: and a neonatal mode, which uses a smaller air volume for cuff inflation and is accurate in the neonate.
paragraphs.heading: Operating Room Equipment and Monitoring

paragraphs.text: Invasive arterial blood pressure measurements from an indwelling line should be considered in sicker or more premature infants. Common sites are the umbilical artery or the radial artery. The arterial line site needs to be considered in relation to the clinical condition of the neonate; if coarctation of the aorta is present, a right radial line should be used. Similarly, if a right Blalock-Taussig shunt is planned, a left radial line is appropriate. Invasive arterial pressure lines allow for monitoring of arterial blood gases as necessary. Arterial lines in the neonate must be treated with the greatest delicacy. If blood is drawn from the line, a small syringe should be used, and suction should never be applied, because the artery easily can go into spasm. The line always should be flushed gently, again with a syringe and not with a pressure bag attached to the transducer. For smaller neonates, an intravenous infusion pump (not a pressure bag) should be used to keep a continuous flow through the transducer, to prevent inadvertent flushing, and to limit the rate of fluid administration through the transducer (3 mL/h with the pressure bag vs. 0.5 mL/h with the pump). Central venous pressure monitoring is infrequently used in premature neonates due to the size of the patient, but it may be used in larger neonates undergoing surgical procedures where significant fluid shifts are expected or during neonatal cardiac surgery.
paragraphs.heading: Operating Room Equipment and Monitoring

paragraphs.text: End-tidal CO2 measurements also have become a standard of care in the operating room, but obtaining accurate measurements in a small neonate can be difficult. With a typical capnograph, the accuracy depends on the actual site of sampling, the type of anesthesia circuit used, and the volume of fresh gas flow through the circuit. The most accurate measurements are obtained using a low dead space circuit, with the sampling site in the endotracheal tube, not on the circuit. Dead spaces within the anesthesia circuit or due to the addition of capnography samplers into a neonatal
paragraphs.heading: Operating Room Equipment and Monitoring

paragraphs.text: circuit, along with low tidal volumes, high respiratory rates, and short exhalation times, limit the accuracy of the quantitative end-tidal CO2 data.34 Although waveform capnography in neonates may not be as accurate with regard to correlation with PaCO2, the qualitative data obtained from the presence of waveform capnography allow for continual confirmation of endotracheal intubation during operative procedures when access to the patient may be limited. Transcutaneous CO2 monitoring is used with increased frequency in the NICU but is not used routinely in the operating room.
paragraphs.heading: Operating Room Equipment and Monitoring

paragraphs.text: Cerebral oximetry employing near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) can provide information on changes in cerebral blood flow and can provide real-time measurement of cerebral tissue oxygenation. In neonatal patients where invasive arterial monitoring can be challenging and lower limits of acceptable blood pressure in anesthetized neonates are unknown, the ability to detect changes in cerebral tissue oxygenation in these vulnerable patients can provide helpful information. NIRS monitoring is used routinely in pediatric cardiac surgery, pediatric intensive care units (PICUs), and NICUs, but we do not have sufficient data to determine if large-scale use of NIRS monitoring in neonates under anesthesia can have an effect on neurodevelopmental outcome.35 Previously, many anesthesia machines were equipped with a rudimentary, volume-limited, time-cycled ventilator, which even with a pediatric bellows was poorly suited for neonatal ventilation. Small tidal volumes were very difficult to set, and tidal volume and pressure varied tremendously depending on the fresh gas flow. In the best of hands, these ventilators are impossible to use with premature neonates. Newer anesthesia machines incorporate significantly more sophisticated ventilators, capable of either volume-limited or pressure-limited ventilation. These ventilators can be used in pressure-limited, time-cycled mode, and they incorporate a spirometer that can measure expired tidal volumes as small as10 mL. Fresh gas flow is uncoupled from tidal volume, and changes in flows do not affect ventilation. PEEP can easily be added without the external valves used in older machines. These machines can be used routinely in infants weighing as little as 1000 g.
paragraphs.heading: Operating Room Equipment and Monitoring

paragraphs.text: An alternative method is to bring a NICU ventilator to the operating room. Critically ill neonates with high ventilator settings may be best served by the accuracy of a NICU ventilator. Using a neonatal ventilator does prevent the use of inhalational anesthetic agents that can only be delivered from an anesthesia machine, so a total intravenous anesthetic technique is necessary.
paragraphs.heading: Operating Room Equipment and Monitoring

paragraphs.text: The circle breathing system, with inspiratory and expiratory valves and incorporating a CO2 absorber, has become standard in adult anesthesia. A major advantage is that a semi-closed technique with very low gas flows can be used, conserving anesthetic agent. Similar circle systems, appropriately sized for infants with lower compliance tubing and smaller bags, are commonly used in neonates.
paragraphs.heading: Operating Room Equipment and Monitoring

paragraphs.text: The operating room must be equipped with appropriately sized airway equipment, including Miller No. 00, 0,
paragraphs.heading: Operating Room Equipment and Monitoring

paragraphs.text: and 1 blades; cuffed and uncuffed endotracheal tubes; and nasopharyngeal and oropharyngeal airways. An assortment of special blades should be available for difficult airway cases. The laryngeal mask airway (LMA) is a device that fits in the pharynx, covering the glottis and the esophageal opening. A cuff seals against the walls of the pharynx. LMAs do not occlude the esophagus and may notably increase the risk of aspiration during positive-pressure ventilation. The smallest LMA available is a size 1 and can be used in neonates <5 kg. LMAs can be very helpful in assisting with ventilation and intubation in some infants with congenital anomalies such as Pierre Robin syndrome, where securing the airway may be difficult. The LMA can be inserted as a temporary method to more easily support positive-pressure ventilation while preparations are made for endotracheal intubation. When an LMA has been positioned, a fiberoptic bronchoscope may be able to be passed through the LMA and into the trachea. An endotracheal tube can be passed through the LMA over the bronchoscope. The neonatal fiberoptic bronchoscope is essential for difficult airway cases. This bronchoscope is limited by extreme flexibility, and it does not have a suction channel, but it passes through a 2.5 endotracheal tube.
paragraphs.heading: Operating Room Equipment and Monitoring

paragraphs.text: Most infants who require surgery receive a general anesthetic. There is increasing interest in regional techniques, but most often this is still combined with a general anesthetic in order to provide for a still surgical field. Successful delivery of general anesthesia in neonates requires knowledge of developmental pharmacology to predict and understand the responses of premature infants to anesthetic drugs. Size has an effect on response to anesthetics, and developmental age has a profound impact on the dose-response, distribution, and metabolism of these drugs.
paragraphs.heading: General Anesthesia for the Neonate

paragraphs.text: Inhalational anesthetics agents include the halogenated volatile anesthetics (sevoflurane, isoflurane, and desflurane) and nitrous oxide. These potent anesthetic gases are delivered via vaporizers into specialized airway circuits connected to anesthesia machines. When delivered into the lungs, these gases are taken up into the bloodstream in order to reach the central nervous system, where they exert their effects.
paragraphs.heading: Inhalational Agents

paragraphs.text: Careful administration of inhaled anesthetics can allow for safe use of these drugs during the maintenance phase of anesthesia. The anesthetic effect of inhalational agents depends on the partial pressure of the anesthetic in the brain and the potency of the agent. For several reasons, very high partial pressures of the inhalational agents in the brain develop much more rapidly in neonates than in older children and adults. First, as already discussed, the ratio of alveolar ventilation (per minute) to FRC in neonates is 5:1 compared with 1.5:1 in adults; consequently, alveolar anesthetic concentration equilibrates with inspired concentration very quickly. Second, a greater fraction of the cardiac
paragraphs.heading: Inhalational Agents

paragraphs.text: output in the neonate is distributed to the vessel-rich group and consequently the brain. Finally, the solubility of the inhaled anesthetics in blood is less in neonates than in adults.
paragraphs.heading: Inhalational Agents

paragraphs.text: Sevoflurane and isoflurane are most commonly used in neonates. Volatile anesthetics are complete anesthetics, with analgesic and amnesic properties. SVR is decreased by isoflurane and hypotension can result, especially if preload is diminished. Moderate volume loading helps to minimize any decrease in blood pressure. Isoflurane also causes cerebral vasodilation, and, in the absence of hypotension, cerebral blood flow increases. In adults, isoflurane decreases cerebral metabolism and is cerebral protective.
paragraphs.heading: Inhalational Agents

paragraphs.text: Sevoflurane has become very popular in pediatric anesthesia due to its usefulness for inhalation induction. It is not irritating to the airway, and it is almost insoluble in blood so that equilibration between brain and alveolus occurs rapidly. Onset of anesthesia during mask induction is very fast and may be used for mask induction in healthier neonates. Cardiovascular effects are similar to effects with isoflurane. Sevoflurane has been associated with prolongation of the Q-T interval of the ECG in adults and infants.
paragraphs.heading: Inhalational Agents

paragraphs.text: In the neonate, inhaled anesthetics are most commonly used during the maintenance phase of anesthesia after intravenous anesthetics are used for the induction phase. Rarely, if a neonate presents to the operating room without intravenous access, the inhalation agent sevoflurane can be administered in higher concentrations to perform an inhalation induction of anesthesia. Isoflurane is very pungent and cannot be used for mask induction. Higher doses of volatile anesthetics required for an inhalation induction may be poorly tolerated, causing hypotension, bradycardia, and decreased cardiac output. Brain tissue equilibrates very quickly with the alveolar concentration of anesthetic, increasing the risk of overdose in a neonate.
paragraphs.heading: Inhalational Agents

paragraphs.text: The potency of inhalational anesthetics is expressed using the minimum alveolar concentration (MAC). The MAC is the concentration at which 50% of patients exhibit no response to surgical stimulation such as skin incision. The MAC is related to PCA and is lowest in very premature neonates, increasing to a peak at a PCA of approximately 1 year and then decreasing progressively from childhood through adulthood. Fig. 39.2 shows this relationship for isoflurane.36 Isoflurane is more potent (lower MAC) in premature neonates than in older infants.
paragraphs.heading: Inhalational Agents

paragraphs.text: Nitrous oxide is an inhalational anesthetic, but it is not in the same class as the halogenated agents. It is a weak anesthetic, with a MAC of 104% in adults; in order to reach MAC, nitrous oxide would have to be provided at hyperbaric pressures in addition to utilizing hypoxic mixtures of gas. The need for oxygen as part of inspired gases prevents achievement of these levels. Nitrous oxide is almost insoluble, and the onset of effect is fast. These properties cause nitrous oxide to progressively enter and expand any gasfilled space in contact with the circulation, which rapidly leads to bowel distention or expansion of pneumothorax. If ventilation is interrupted for any reason, nitrous oxide
paragraphs.heading: Inhalational Agents

paragraphs.text: also rapidly fills the alveoli, leading to dilution of the alveolar oxygen, producing a hypoxic mixture and rapid desaturation. For these reasons, nitrous oxide is best limited to adjunct use during mask induction, with a switch to an airoxygen mixture during maintenance anesthesia, and it has limited usefulness in the anesthetic management of the neonate. As previously discussed, all of the inhalational agents cause neuroapoptosis in animal studies.
paragraphs.heading: Inhalational Agents

paragraphs.text: Intravenous anesthetic agents for use in neonates include propofol, ketamine, opioids, and benzodiazepines. Propofol is a phenol derivative supplied as an emulsion in lipid, which is used for induction and maintenance of anesthesia. Recovery from the drug is rapid due to redistribution and metabolism by liver and tissues. Propofol has few analgesic effects, and for painful operations it should be used with additional analgesics. Propofol has been approved for children over 2 months of age, but great care must be taken when administering it due to significant interindividual variability, especially at extremes of age. Larger initial doses (2–3 mg/kg) are often necessary in neonates due to a larger volume of extracellular fluid, but they exhibit a slower recovery due to less fat and muscle for redistribution, as well as slower hepatic metabolism due to immaturity. When used as an infusion, dosing should be decreased in neonates to account for slower clearance.37 It is a potent peripheral vasodilator, and significant protracted hypotension after bolus dosing is a common problem limiting its use in preterm neonates.38
paragraphs.heading: Intravenous Agents

paragraphs.text: Ketamine is a phencyclidine derivative that acts as an N-methyl-d-aspartate (NMDA) receptor antagonist; it provides good hypnosis and amnesia and excellent analgesia. When used as a sole agent in adults and older children, it can cause a dissociative state with confusion, hallucinations, and other severe psychological side effects. Ketamine stimulates the sympathetic nervous system and causes minimal
paragraphs.heading: Intravenous Agents

paragraphs.text: respiratory and cardiovascular depression, which may make it a useful adjunct in the anesthetic care of the infant. Blood pressure may increase, and increased intracranial pressure is a concern in infants with hydrocephalus or those at risk for intraventricular hemorrhage. Ketamine can be useful in breaking hypercyanotic spells caused by increased right-toleft shunting in infants with tetralogy of Fallot, because it anesthetizes and increases SVR.
paragraphs.heading: Intravenous Agents

paragraphs.text: Benzodiazepines are agents that produce sedation, anxiolysis, and amnesia, but little analgesia. They are incomplete anesthetic agents, although in adults they have been very useful in combination with an opioid. Midazolam is a very short-acting benzodiazepine, and it has been the most commonly used in anesthesia. Metabolism is almost entirely hepatic, and it should be expected that duration would be prolonged by immature hepatic function in a preterm neonate. Midazolam causes vasodilation, which can result in hypotension. In high doses, it can cause respiratory depression, although this is more common in conjunction with opioids. Midazolam and the longer-acting benzodiazepine lorazepam have been used for sedation in the NICU with mixed results. The Cochrane Neonatal Collaborative Review Group performed a meta-analysis of several studies on sedation in the NICU using midazolam. All three studies showed that midazolam was effective at providing sedation to the neonate. However, one study showed a higher risk of poor neurologic outcome or death in the midazolam-treated group, as well as evidence of increased length of stay, which at least raises questions as to the safety of midazolam infusion in these infants.39
paragraphs.heading: Intravenous Agents

paragraphs.text: Morphine is the principal opium alkaloid, and it is the standard against which analgesics are measured. Morphine is less potent than fentanyl, but it has a longer duration of action and is more commonly used for postoperative pain. Due to immature hepatic metabolism, the duration of action of morphine is increased in premature infants which should be taken into account when determining the frequency of intermittent boluses. As with all opioids, respiratory depression is a major side effect. In contrast to fentanyl, morphine causes histamine release, which limits the ability to use it in high doses as an anesthetic agent, although it is well accepted for analgesia, postoperative pain, and overall sedation. Morphine distribution in neonates has been well studied and is very predictable, although required target concentrations in neonates are still uncertain.
paragraphs.heading: Intravenous Agents

paragraphs.text: Fentanyl, a synthetic opioid, is widely used in neonatal anesthesia, and it is the most commonly used anesthetic for premature infants. It has a wide safety margin and beneficial effects on hemodynamic stability. Fentanyl can block pulmonary hypertensive crises, and it is useful in infants with pulmonary hypertension, such as infants with congenital diaphragmatic hernia, PPHN, and some cardiac defects. The pharmacokinetics of fentanyl in the early neonatal period is widely variable, depending on gestational and postnatal age and the type of surgery and medical comorbidities of the infant. Fentanyl is primarily metabolized in the liver, with only a small amount excreted unchanged by the kidneys.
paragraphs.heading: Intravenous Agents

paragraphs.text: Clearance is lowest in the most premature infants, and it increases with gestational age and with age after birth, probably reflecting increasing hepatic maturation. Volume of distribution of fentanyl also seems to vary depending on gestational age and disease state. Neonates with increased intra-abdominal pressure seem to have slower clearance of fentanyl, likely due to the resulting decreased hepatic blood flow.
paragraphs.heading: Intravenous Agents

paragraphs.text: Given the highly variable pharmacodynamics, fentanyl dosing should start low (0.25 μg/kg) and be titrated to clinical effect. There is a fairly wide therapeutic range, and even with high doses, hemodynamic stability is maintained. All narcotics are respiratory depressants, however, and with higher doses of fentanyl, prolonged respiratory depression occurs, necessitating postoperative assisted ventilation.
paragraphs.heading: Intravenous Agents

paragraphs.text: Fentanyl in combination with a muscle relaxant has become the standard for anesthesia in very premature neonates. This combination may also be used during elective (nonemergent) intubation in the NICU. Although fentanyl is a potent analgesic, it is not a complete anesthetic, and occasionally in adults, awareness has occurred with high-dose fentanyl alone. In the past, it was suggested that this was of minimal importance because neonates are not “aware,” especially if pain was adequately treated. This belief is less well accepted today, and benzodiazepines or inhalational agents such as isoflurane are more commonly added to fentanyl anesthesia in the operating room.
paragraphs.heading: Intravenous Agents

paragraphs.text: Other synthetic narcotics such as alfentanil and sufentanil rarely have been used in neonates. In adults, alfentanil is less potent than fentanyl, but it has a shorter half-life, whereas sufentanil is more potent than fentanyl. The pharmacokinetics in infants is probably similar to fentanyl, and there does not seem to be any significant advantage compared with fentanyl. Remifentanil is a newer opioid whose duration of action is terminated by hydrolysis by tissue esterases. Consequently, remifentanil does not accumulate or have prolonged duration of action. A half-life of 4.4 minutes and a clearance of 80 mL/kg/min have been reported in neonates.40 Duration of action is very short, and it may be of use for procedural analgesia with little persistent pain. Duration can be extended by using a continuous infusion, but this can be associated with opioid-induced tolerance and hyperalgesia.40,41
paragraphs.heading: Intravenous Agents

paragraphs.text: Acetaminophen is one of the most commonly used analgesic medications for neonates. Acetaminophen is considered to be a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID), and it exerts its analgesic effects via inhibition of cyclooxygenase enzymes and decreasing prostaglandin synthesis. It has frequently been used as an adjunct for pain relief postoperatively, and its use after major abdominal or thoracic procedures is associated with a decrease in opioid consumption.42 Previously, the use of acetaminophen intraoperatively was limited to the rectal route of administration which is known to have variable uptake and effectiveness. However, the availability of an intravenous formulation has allowed for the routine use of acetaminophen intraoperatively as an adjunct analgesic. Dosing should be adjusted based on PCA
paragraphs.heading: Intravenous Agents

paragraphs.text: (7.5–10 mg/kg for patients <36 weeks’ PCA) to avoid the risk of hepatic toxicity, as clearance of the drug is lower.43
paragraphs.heading: Intravenous Agents

paragraphs.text: Dexmedetomidine is a highly specific alpha2-adrenergic agonist with hypnotic, analgesic, and anxiolytic properties. It is being used with increased frequency in the pediatric setting for sedation during nonpainful procedures such as MRI, as an adjunct to other anesthetics during surgical procedures, and for sedation of critically ill patients in the ICU setting. Despite the sedating properties of dexmedetomidine, there is little effect on respiratory function, thereby promoting earlier extubation and decreasing the need for analgesics that have respiratory depressant properties. Numerous studies have demonstrated the effectiveness and safety of dexmedetomidine as an analgesic and sedative in infants after cardiac surgery. Adverse effects of dexmedetomidine include bradycardia and hypotension, as well as paradoxical hypertension, but it has been found to be well tolerated in neonates.44 The drug undergoes hepatic metabolism and therefore has decreased plasma clearance and a longer elimination half-life in preterm neonates with immature hepatocyte function.45 Preliminary data in animal studies show evidence that dexmedetomidine may actually protect against neuroapoptosis caused by other anesthetic agents.46
paragraphs.heading: Intravenous Agents

paragraphs.text: Muscle relaxants are commonly used in anesthesia for neonates. They are often grouped according to mechanism of action (i.e., depolarizing vs. nondepolarizing), but it is more important to consider rapidity of onset and duration of action. Succinylcholine is the only depolarizing agent used at present, and it remains the standard for rapid onset and rapid disappearance. The ED95 (effective dose in 95% of the population receiving the dose) in neonates for succinylcholine is at least twice that of adults at 2 to 3 mg/ kg. Action is terminated by metabolism by plasma pseudocholinesterase. Succinylcholine is not routinely used in children because of several rare but serious adverse reactions. In patients with myopathies or neurologic diseases, succinylcholine can cause overwhelming hyperkalemia, muscle necrosis, and cardiac arrest that is refractory to resuscitation. Bradycardia also occasionally occurs during intubation in infants with succinylcholine. For this reason, some anesthesiologists routinely administer atropine with succinylcholine. In pediatric patients, succinylcholine is reserved primarily for rapid sequence induction when a full stomach is suspected.
paragraphs.heading: Neuromuscular Blocking Agents

paragraphs.text: Nondepolarizing relaxants competitively inhibit acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction. Vecuronium bromide is an intermediate-acting relaxant occasionally used in neonates. It has little effect on the cardiac system, although it may cause bradycardia in combination with narcotics. Cisatracurium besylate undergoes spontaneous degradation by a chemical process (Hofmann elimination), and duration is not affected by liver or kidney function. Rocuronium bromide is an agent with a rapid onset of action that can be used in place of succinylcholine for rapid sequence
paragraphs.heading: Neuromuscular Blocking Agents

paragraphs.text: induction. Duration of action is dose dependent and significantly longer than succinylcholine.
paragraphs.heading: Neuromuscular Blocking Agents

paragraphs.text: Most relaxants probably have a prolonged duration of action in premature neonates, and frequency of dosing should be determined using a nerve stimulator to measure response to four spaced stimuli (train-of-four response). This type of monitoring can be challenging with small premature neonates. At the completion of surgery, muscle relaxation with nondepolarizing agents should be reversed. An anticholinesterase, typically neostigmine, and an anticholinergic, such as glycopyrrolate or atropine, can be used for reversal. Sugammadex, a newer reversal agent for the commonly used muscle relaxants rocuronium and vecuronium, is currently approved as a reversal agent in children over 2 years old. However, there are a number of cases series of sugammadex being used “off-label” in neonates and infants without significant adverse events.47 Sugammadex has the benefit of being able to reverse profound neuromuscular blockade (unlike neostigmine), but further studies are needed to confirm its safety in neonates.
paragraphs.heading: Neuromuscular Blocking Agents

paragraphs.text: Most sick infants have intravenous access, and an intravenous induction can be performed. Premedication rarely is given to neonates, although some anesthesiologists recommend glycopyrrolate or atropine before laryngoscopy and intubation to mitigate any possible vagal response and bradycardia with intubation. Healthier infants without intravenous access can undergo mask induction, typically with 50% nitrous oxide and sevoflurane, after which intravenous access is rapidly obtained.
paragraphs.heading: Induction of General Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: Infants with a full stomach, most commonly infants with intra-abdominal disease, must have an intravenous rapidsequence induction. During rapid-sequence induction, the infant is first preoxygenated with 100% FiO2 to maximize oxygenation during the apneic period of intubation. An intravenous induction agent such as propofol, along with a fast-acting paralytic, is administered in rapid succession. The use of cricoid pressure to prevent regurgitation of gastric contents is not routinely considered, as it can actually hinder successful intubation by obscuring the view of the glottic opening during laryngoscopy.48 Positive-pressure ventilation is avoided or provided very gently, and the infant is intubated expertly as soon as conditions are appropriate, usually after 45 to 90 seconds. There is little room for error with rapid sequence induction, and it should be performed only by individuals with significant expertise.
paragraphs.heading: Induction of General Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: Maintenance of spontaneous ventilation may be considered if there is significant concern for a difficult airway, such as in Pierre Robin and Goldenhar syndromes. Maintenance of spontaneous ventilation is beneficial during situations where mask ventilation may be difficult and time to successful intubation may be prolonged. When the airway is secured, muscle relaxation can be administered as necessary. In the past, awake intubations were often considered when a difficult airway was suspected in order to maintain spontaneous ventilation and airway reflexes. However,
paragraphs.heading: Induction of General Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: awake intubations are now known to cause higher rates of airway trauma and can have significant hemodynamic consequences in the neonate such as arterial hypertension, pulmonary hypertensive crisis, and increased intracranial pressure due to pain and sympathetic stimulation.49 This technique is rarely used in the operating room.
paragraphs.heading: Induction of General Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: When the potential for a difficult airway exists, careful planning is necessary to ensure the availability of specialty equipment, as well as the availability of additional “trained hands.” Intubation should occur in a controlled manner whenever possible, and elective intubation should be considered early to avoid emergency airway situations. A pediatric fiberoptic bronchoscope and a range of special-purpose laryngoscope blades may be useful. LMAs should be available to assist with ventilation, but they do not protect the airway from aspiration. The pediatric bronchoscope also can be used to intubate through the LMA. Video laryngoscopes may be helpful, especially in the setting of intubation by trainees. Pediatric ear, nose, and throat consultation may also be necessary for expertise in rigid bronchoscopy.
paragraphs.heading: Induction of General Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: Concerns about the neurotoxicity of general anesthetic agents and widespread availability of ultrasound have resulted in increased interest in regional anesthesia in children and neonates. Ultrasound has made it both easier and safer to perform regional blocks in children. Regional anesthesia techniques include local infiltration, fascial plane blocks, peripheral nerve blocks, and neuraxial anesthesia. Regional techniques are commonly combined with general anesthesia, with the goals of reducing intraoperative anesthetic requirements, decreasing postoperative analgesic requirements, and promoting earlier extubation. Analysis of data from the Pediatric Regional Anesthesia Network (PRAN) comprised of more than 100,000 blocks demonstrated that the risk of major complications when performing regional anesthesia on anesthetized children is exceedingly rare, with no permanent neurologic deficits reported.50 This analysis included almost 10,000 regional anesthetics in neonates and infants. There are inherent technical difficulties to performing regional anesthesia in neonates, including the need for appropriate-sized catheters and the need for specialized training to perform these blocks safely and successfully. However, there are numerous reports of safe and effective administration of regional anesthesia in neonates.
paragraphs.heading: Regional Anesthesia and Local Anesthetics

paragraphs.text: Local infiltration or distal nerve block is useful in certain specific procedures such as circumcision, where a dorsal penile nerve block (DPNB) or penile ring block has been shown to be effective as a sole anesthetic. Other simple methods, such as a sucrose-dipped pacifier or a padded and physiologic restraint chair, further decrease objective signs of distress during circumcision performed with DPNB. A eutectic mixture of local anesthetic (EMLA) cream also has been used for neonatal circumcision. Other indications for use of EMLA include venous and arterial puncture,
paragraphs.heading: Regional Anesthesia and Local Anesthetics

paragraphs.text: lumbar puncture, suprapubic puncture, and minor surgical procedures.
paragraphs.heading: Regional Anesthesia and Local Anesthetics

paragraphs.text: Neuraxial regional anesthetic techniques include epidural and spinal anesthesia. Neuraxial anesthesia aims to make an area of the body insensate through the administration of local anesthetic into either the intrathecal or epidural space. In neonates and infants, the epidural space can be easily entered by the caudal route through the sacrococcygeal membrane (Fig. 39.3). Caudal anesthesia is a useful option for surgeries involving the lower abdomen, groin, and lower extremities. Caudal anesthesia given as a single injection is commonly used in combination with a general anesthetic to allow for lower concentrations of inhalational agents and provide postoperative pain control, but it can occasionally be used as the sole anesthetic. After a caudal anesthetic with bupivacaine or ropivacaine, most infants are free of pain immediately after surgery, with relief continuing for at least 4 hours. The single-shot technique utilizes a 22-gauge, short-bevel needle or 22-gauge angiocath to enter the caudal space. Caudal anesthesia requires a higher dosage of local anesthetic than a spinal anesthetic, so the possibility of an inadvertent intravascular injection is a concern.
paragraphs.heading: Regional Anesthesia and Local Anesthetics

paragraphs.text: A catheter can also be threaded via the caudal route up to the thoracic epidural space or it can be inserted and threaded directly into the thoracic or lumbar epidural space if continuous analgesia is needed for multiple days. Epidural catheters allow for the continuous infusion of local anesthetic intra- and postoperatively, thereby minimizing the need for analgesics that may result in respiratory depression or may have altered pharmacokinetic properties in the immature neonate. This technique is well tolerated without significant hemodynamic effect. Despite the ability to perform these procedures, there has long been concern over the safety of these techniques in the neonatal patient. An observational study utilizing the PRAN was able to evaluate the incidence of complications related to the use of neuraxial catheters in patients under 1 month of age. With over 300 neuraxial catheters placed, the most common complications were catheter malfunction, catheter contamination, and vascular aspiration, all of which were managed by removal or adjustment of the catheter. There were no reports of more serious complications, such as persistent neurologic injury, deep infection, or epidural hematoma.51
paragraphs.heading: Regional Anesthesia and Local Anesthetics

paragraphs.text: With the increased use of ultrasound for regional anesthesia, truncal or fascial plane blocks have been gaining popularity. The injection and spread of local anesthetic within a fascial plane targets nerves traveling within the plane and adjacent tissue. They are less invasive than neuraxial techniques and appear to be low risk, as local anesthetic is injected into a fascial plane, which avoids larger nerve bundles or the neuraxial space. These fascial plane blocks are relatively easy to perform in neonates compared to more challenging neuraxial techniques. They are most commonly performed for anesthetic coverage of thoracic and abdominal incisions. Table 39.4 compares common fascial plane blocks with their indications.
paragraphs.heading: Regional Anesthesia and Local Anesthetics

paragraphs.text: Regional anesthesia in the pediatric patient is most commonly performed under general anesthesia with an exceedingly low complication rate.50 A regional technique without general anesthesia can be used in some neonates considered to be at high risk, such as those with severe BPD, in whom avoidance of intubation for a general anesthetic is preferred in addition to avoiding the potential negative effects of anesthesia on neurocognitive development.52 Despite the avoidance of a general anesthetic, the most robust study comparing general anesthesia to awake regional anesthesia did not reveal an overall reduction in postoperative apnea in those patients receiving a regional anesthetic, but the infants receiving spinal anesthesia had fewer clinically significant apneas.53 Spinal anesthesia can be performed using a 25-gauge Quincke needle at the L4 or L5 level (below the cauda equina). Either tetracaine or bupivacaine can be injected into the intrathecal space to provide a dense block up to the T5–T6 dermatome. This type of block can be used for procedures performed on the lower abdomen, groin, or lower extremities. Inguinal hernia repair is a common neonatal surgical procedure where spinal anesthesia can be successfully used. Due to the duration of the block, surgical procedures must be completed in less than 90 minutes in order for spinal anesthesia to be considered. Addition of adjuncts such as clonidine may be able to increase to length of the block up to 100 minutes.54 Caudal or spinal anesthesia can be used with or without additional sedation. Simple
paragraphs.heading: Regional Anesthesia and Local Anesthetics

paragraphs.text: nonpharmacologic comfort measures such as a pacifier and sucrose solution are often adequate to allow tolerance of the procedure.
paragraphs.heading: Regional Anesthesia and Local Anesthetics

paragraphs.text: Commonly used local anesthetics for regional anesthesia in neonates and infants include bupivacaine, ropivacaine, 2-chloroprocaine, and tetracaine. Careful attention must be paid to the dosing of local anesthetics, especially with the use of continuous epidural infusions, to avoid potentially toxic doses. Many local anesthetics are metabolized by hepatic enzymes that are immature in the neonate. These physiologic differences place neonates and infants at higher risk for local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST), as reduced clearance can result in local anesthetic accumulation. Maximum dosages of local anesthetics are reduced in neonates and infants to minimize the risk of toxicity. The use of 2-chloroprocaine for continuous infusions may reduce the risk of LAST, as it is metabolized by plasma cholinesterase, resulting in a much shorter half-life.55
paragraphs.heading: Regional Anesthesia and Local Anesthetics

paragraphs.text: Maintenance of anesthesia requires full monitoring throughout with, at a minimum, continuous ECG, pulse oximetry, and end-tidal CO2 as well as frequent noninvasive blood pressure monitoring. Temperature should also be monitored and must be carefully controlled with adjustments in heating or cooling as appropriate. Fluid and metabolic requirements also must be carefully assessed throughout the course of the surgery. Fluids should be administered with an infusion pump to prevent inadvertent fluid overload. It is usually easiest to calculate and administer maintenance fluids separately from replacement. Maintenance fluids should include glucose unless the infant is known to be hyperglycemic. Intravenous hyperalimentation or a dextrose-electrolyte solution can be used, depending on the size, age, and clinical condition of the neonate. Intraoperatively, glucose requirements are often lower than normal maintenance requirements, as surgical stress results in increased catecholamine and cortisol levels and decreased plasma insulin with resulting hyperglycemia. Care should be taken to avoid interruptions in glucose-containing infusions and to monitor blood glucose levels when surgical procedures exceed 2 to 3 hours. Hyperglycemia can be minimized intraoperatively
paragraphs.heading: Maintenance of Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: by using lower concentrations of dextrose in fluids such as 2.5% dextrose.56 Isotonic fluids should be used preferably for fluid repletion to avoid hyponatremia postoperatively. Third-space losses should be initially replaced with a balanced crystalloid solution such as lactated Ringer’s. Blood loss also can be replaced with crystalloid initially.
paragraphs.heading: Maintenance of Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: Third-space losses can be impressive, ranging from 2 to 15 mL/kg/h, especially during procedures with large amounts of bowel exposed, such as for repair of gastroschisis and omphalocele or bowel resection. Many infants, especially if they are hypoalbuminemic, should receive some replacement as colloids, usually 5% albumin. Transfusion with packed red blood cells, fresh frozen plasma, and platelets may be required. If significant surgical blood loss is anticipated, blood products should be prepared prior to the start of surgery in order to ensure that products can be appropriately prepared. Packed red blood cells should be washed, leukoreduced, and irradiated prior to transfusion. Blood products should be administered in small aliquots, ideally from a single donor if possible. Urine output should be followed as one sign of adequate fluid replacement.
paragraphs.heading: Maintenance of Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: Ventilation should be carefully controlled. Use of oxygen has been discussed; if controlled ventilation is employed, care should be taken to avoid hyperventilation and subsequent hypocapnia. Higher peak pressures can cause significant barotrauma. Accurate ventilation may be difficult to monitor because varying anesthesia circuits and adapters can result in widely varying dead space and a variable offset between end-tidal CO2 and the actual blood partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PCO2). Premature neonates, especially those less than 1500 g, often benefit from the use of an ICU ventilator for better accuracy of delivered volumes.
paragraphs.heading: Maintenance of Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: Emergence from anesthesia in the smallest and sickest premature infants may be a prolonged event, and these neonates are not typical candidates for extubation at the conclusion of surgery; instead, they require continued intensive care in the NICU. Immaturity of drug clearance systems also prolongs recovery from the effects of most anesthetic agents in these infants. Older and healthier neonates, even those that are premature, can often be extubated after many types
paragraphs.heading: Recovery From Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: of surgical procedures, but most still require recovery and monitoring in an intensive care setting. Neuromuscular blockade should be reversed, as previously discussed. Hypothermia can prolong neuromuscular blockade, precluding extubation if temperature control has not been adequate, and infants with hypothermia may need to be actively warmed. Transport from the operating room involves the same considerations of temperature maintenance and airway management that have previously been discussed.
paragraphs.heading: Recovery From Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: The infant should resume regular rhythmic respiration; to achieve this, ventilation may have to be decreased toward the end of the anesthetic to allow the PCO2 to increase to mildly hypercapnic levels. Volume status must be adequate, and plasma hemoglobin should be close to normal. Flexion
paragraphs.heading: Recovery From Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: • The goals of anesthesia care in the neonate include man-

paragraphs.text: agement of pain and discomfort associated with surgical procedures and prevention of the stress response. • Animal studies have demonstrated abnormal apoptosis
paragraphs.heading: Recovery From Anesthesia
