39 Anesthesia in the Neonate

### SHELLEY OHLIGER

### Safety and Challenges of Neonatal Anesthesia

The administration of anesthesia to the neonatal patient requires knowledge and understanding of neonatal anatomy and pathophysiology in addition to the ability to understand how the pharmacology of standard anesthetic drugs is altered in preterm and term neonates. Perioperative surgical anesthetic risk in children increases with decreasing age, making neonatal patients some of the most vulnerable patients anesthesiologists provide anesthetic care for. Anesthesia for these oftentimes critical patients is best performed by specialty-trained pediatric anesthesiologists, as anesthesia-related morbidity is reduced in children anesthetized by pediatric anesthesiologists compared with children cared for by non-pediatric anesthesiologists.1 The American College of Surgeons has developed standards recommending that children under the age of 2 years have anesthesia administered by a pediatric specialty-trained anesthesiologist.2

The goals of neonatal anesthesia are similar to those in adults but require different skills, knowledge, and care. The differences between adults and children are most profound in neonates, particularly premature infants. Advances in neonatology and the almost routine survival of infants weighing greater than 1000 g have led to new challenges for pediatric anesthesiologists. Successful anesthetic management in a neonate requires meticulous attention to detail and a thorough understanding of neonatal physiology and development, pharmacology, and pathophysiology. The neonatal period is characterized by immaturity of organ systems, homeostasis, and metabolic pathways. It is a time of major developmental changes, and the effects of anesthesia on that development are not well characterized. Knowledge of the anatomic and physiologic differences among neonates, children, and adults is critical to careful anesthetic administration and management. Maturity of organ systems and metabolic processes varies significantly not only between adults and neonates but also between preterm and term neonates.

Personnel, equipment, and the operating room environment need to be specifically adapted for neonates. Monitors, anesthesia delivery systems, mechanical ventilators,

and environmental controls all need to be appropriate for use with neonates.

It is important to emphasize the perioperative nature of anesthetic management. Anesthesia care does not start and end at the door to the operative suite, and this is as critical in neonates as in older children and adults. Preoperative medical status and current medical management strategies can affect intraoperative care. Transport to the operating room can be one of the most critical aspects of an operation in a premature neonate. The postoperative period requires close monitoring and management of ventilation, fluid balance, and an environment tailored to the special needs of neonates. Assessment and control of postoperative pain require methods and tools specific to neonates.

Surgery in neonates is accompanied by a humoral stress response that, left untreated, leads to increased complications and mortality, as shown in the landmark study by Anand and colleagues in 1987.3 This response is diminished by adequate anesthesia (Fig. 39.1, Table 39.1), resulting in improved surgical outcomes. Consequently, over the subsequent decades, adequate anesthesia for all surgical procedures in neonates has been accepted as both a clinical and an ethical imperative.

It is also now generally accepted that neonates are capable of sensing pain and discomfort. We have no recallable memories before 3 to 4 years of age (termed infantile amnesia), but neonates do possess consciousness and a sense of self and can form implicit memories—that is, changes in behavior based on prior experience that do not require intentional recall. Plasticity is an inherent characteristic of the developing nervous system, and early pain experiences can lead to exaggerated responses to later painful stimuli or stress, as well as impaired neurodevelopmental outcome.4,5 Activation of brain regions in response to graded moderate pain stimuli is significantly different in school-aged children and adolescents with neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) experience compared with controls, as measured by functional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).6 Based on such evidence, the goals of anesthesia in neonates are not restricted to prevention of the stress response to surgery but also include effective management of pain and discomfort.7,8

In some species, and with some agents, this dose also results in significant mortality, increasing the difficulty of interpreting the significance. Synaptogenesis in rats occurs postnatally over the first 2 weeks of life. An analogous period in humans would range from the third trimester of pregnancy through the first 3 years of life. Whether the child might be susceptible to anesthetic toxicity during this entire period is unknown. Studies in nonhuman primates are assumed to be more translatable to humans. These concerns led the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), as a result of their ongoing initiative, to study the risk of anesthetic exposure on brain development, to publish a warning in 2016 against repeated or lengthy use of general anesthetics and sedation drugs during surgeries and procedures in children younger than 3 years of age or in pregnant women.13

More recent prospective studies with more robust methodology and longer-term follow-up reveal that a single brief anesthetic in early life may have no effect on longterm neurocognitive development. The General Anaesthesia Compared to Spinal Anaesthesia (GAS) study, a prospective randomized controlled trial comparing sevoflurane general anesthesia to awake regional anesthesia (spinal or caudal) for herniorrhaphy in infancy, did not reveal any difference in neurodevelopmental outcome at both 2- and 5-year follow-up.14

The Pediatric Anesthesia and Neurodevelopment Assessment (PANDA) study, a prospective sibling-matched cohort study, compared neurocognitive outcomes in infants receiving a short inhaled general anesthetic for herniorrhaphy to a biological sibling with no anesthetic exposure. Follow-up neuropsychological assessment of sibling pairs at ages varying from 8 to 15 years old showed no difference in neurocognitive outcomes.15 The Mayo Anesthesia Safety in Kids (MASK) study, a matched cohort study of almost 1000 children that underwent neuropsychological testing between the ages of 8 and 12 years old or 15 and 19 years old, found that exposure to general anesthesia during childhood was not associated with deficits in cognition.16 In addition, three large retrospective matched cohorts with greater than 59,000 children combined did not find sufficient data to conclude that young age at initial exposure or multiple anesthetic exposures contributed to adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes.17–19

No one can question the overwhelming benefit of anesthesia in the setting in which a surgical procedure, or any noxious procedure with significant stress, is required. The detrimental effects of surgical stress have been well shown. Similarly, the benefits of early repair of some surgical problems, such as congenital heart defects or neonatal hernia with risk of incarceration, have been shown, although such repair may lead to anesthesia at a younger, and potentially more susceptible, age. When deciding to proceed with an anesthetic, the benefit versus the risk of delay in surgical procedures, particularly if performed in premature infants, should be carefully considered. Reassuringly, current human studies suggest that a short anesthetic exposure during early development is safe.

### Preoperative Evaluation and Preparation

The presence of certain comorbidities along with intrinsic surgical risk play a role in estimating perioperative risk of

morbidity and mortality for all pediatric patients. A retrospective multivariate analysis of over 350,000 surgical cases determined that the presence of the following risk factors in the setting of higher risk surgical procedures was associated with risk for 30-day mortality:20 • Weight <5 kg • American Society of Anesthesiology (ASA) status III or

higher • Preoperative sepsis • Inotropic support • Ventilator dependence prior to surgery

Similar findings were found in the Neonate-Children Study of Anaesthesia Practice in Europe (NECTARINE) study.21 These comorbidities are present in many neonatal patients along with the need for some higher-risk surgical procedures. Understanding the risks undertaken with both the anesthetic and the surgical procedure for a given patient allows for an informed discussion with both families and the neonatology team.

The preoperative evaluation should include the neonate’s current physical condition, including significant illness, the degree of transition from fetal to newborn physiology, maturity, and the presence of any congenital anomalies. Particular attention should be paid to cardiorespiratory status, required ventilatory or hemodynamic support, blood chemistries, and nutritional support.

A full maternal history including the course of pregnancy, labor, and delivery provides important details. A family history of anesthetic difficulties, most importantly a history of malignant hyperthermia or pseudocholinesterase deficiency, must be obtained as these conditions alter the choice of medications that can be used to perform a safe anesthetic. Maternal diseases such as diabetes, systemic lupus erythematosus, and preeclampsia have implications for the neonate. Congenital infections, oligohydramnios, intrauterine growth restriction, and maternal drug and alcohol use are also important considerations.

Gestational age, birth weight, and postnatal age affect anesthetic care. Birth weight does not accurately reflect maturity unless the infant is appropriate for gestational age, which is defined as being within 2 standard deviations of the mean for gestational age. Infants who are small for gestational age are more mature than their birth weight would indicate. Infants who are large for gestational age are often children of diabetic mothers, and they are at increased risk of hypoglycemia in the first 48 hours after birth. A history of birth asphyxia or neonatal resuscitation and Apgar scores can provide information about the health status of the neonate.

Medical history should include complete details of the present illness and treatment. Medications and administration times, details of vascular access, and respiratory parameters including ventilator type and settings all are crucial details, especially in sicker infants. Infants on highfrequency oscillatory ventilation may need to be switched to conventional ventilation and observed for several hours to facilitate movement to an operating room. If the infant

The time of the last oral feed should be noted to assure that appropriate nil per os (NPO, nothing by mouth) guidelines have been met. Attenuation of airway reflexes with induction of anesthesia places the infant at risk for aspiration of acidic gastric contents, which can lead to serious inflammatory pneumonitis. These guidelines are summarized in Table 39.222 and are meant to ensure that the volume and composition of gastric contents are as minimal as possible. However, attempts should be made to avoid longer than necessary NPO times to prevent interruptions in vital nutrition and avoid dehydration. The intake of clear fluids up to 2 hours prior to the induction of anesthesia is actually encouraged, as it can help to avoid fluctuations in blood glucose levels, avoids neonatal distress due to hunger, and improves parental satisfaction. In neonates, dehydration and hypoglycemia occur much more quickly than in older patients, and this risk is even greater in an infant without an intravenous line if NPO times are prolonged.

Gastric emptying is delayed with stress, anxiety, and illness. Infants with diseases such as pyloric stenosis, duodenal atresia, malrotation, or other obstructive lesions are often already NPO leading up to surgery, and they need an intravenous line to maintain appropriate hydration. Despite the NPO status, there usually are significant gastric contents, and rapid-sequence induction and intubation are required if there is any concern for obstruction. Emptying the stomach via nasogastric drainage is undependable and usually inadequate. Gastric feeds even in intubated infants also should be discontinued at an appropriate time because the infant may need to be reintubated during surgery, and a full stomach would increase the risk for aspiration.

Physical examination should include an assessment of vital signs noting trends or recent changes. Careful attention should be paid to evaluation of the cardiorespiratory system. Many neonates requiring surgery are ill and are at risk for hemodynamic or respiratory instability.

The presence of any congenital anomalies must be noted, as they may have an impact on anesthetic care. Often, a group of defects suggests a well-recognized and characterized syndrome. A number of common syndromes with their anesthetic implications are listed in Table 39.3.

Difficult intubation is a common problem in infants with congenital defects, and the airway must be carefully assessed. The presence of micrognathia or retrognathia can be an indicator of a difficult airway. Intraoral, facial or neck masses may make a neonate difficult to both mask ventilate and intubate. Limitations in neck mobility can also affect airway management. Because of the tendency for rapid oxygen desaturation in infants, difficulties with intubation can be extremely serious. In infants who are already intubated, tube size and position should be evaluated. The pressure at which a leak occurs around the tube should be documented. The pulmonary circulation in a neonate is hyperreactive; multiple stressors including surgical stimulation can initiate episodes of pulmonary hypertension, resulting in decreased cardiac output and oxygen desaturation. ### Neonatal Physiology and Specific Anesthetic Concerns

### Transition Phase and Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Neonate

In utero, the pulmonary circulation is a high-resistance circuit so that the lungs receive little blood flow, and oxygenation is a placental function. At birth, amniotic fluid is expelled from the lungs, the lungs expand, and respiration begins. The lungs are initially very stiff (compliance very low), and the first breath may require negative forces of 70 cm H2O or more. Pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) decreases rapidly with lung distention, while oxygenation, pulmonary blood flow, and cardiac output increase. The increase in pulmonary blood flow coupled with decreased venous return from the inferior vena cava with clamping of the placenta causes left atrial pressure to exceed right atrial pressure, resulting in closure of the foramen ovale. The ductus arteriosus should functionally close between 1 and 15 hours after birth.

Although PVR decreases, the pulmonary arterioles possess abundant smooth muscle, and the pulmonary vascular bed remains very reactive. In this setting, hypoxia, hypercarbia, or acidosis can cause a sudden increase in PVR and a return to a fetal circulatory pattern, a condition known as persistent fetal circulation or persistent pulmonary hypertension of the neonate (PPHN). PPHN is an acute, life-threatening condition, as shunt fraction increases to 70% to 80%, and profound cyanosis results. Many factors during anesthesia can affect this transitional state. Anesthetic agents can markedly diminish systemic vascular resistance (SVR), resulting in a right-to-left shunt. Hypoxia or hypercarbia and acidosis from inadequate ventilation can increase PVR. Surgical stimulation and the surgical stress response can cause sympathetic stimulation and a release of catechols that can cause abrupt increases in PVR. Anesthetic care of a neonate, especially in the first few days of life, needs to take into account the reactivity of the pulmonary vascular bed. Pulse oximetry should be monitored in both a pre- and postductal location in order to allow for early identification of PDA shunt reversal if PVR increases. Adequate anesthesia and analgesia must be maintained to prevent excessive catecholamine release. When caring for neonates with known or high risk for pulmonary hypertension, pulmonary vasodilators such as inhaled nitric oxide and options for inotropic support should be immediately available.

### Respiratory Mechanics, Central Control of Ventilation, and Apnea

Compared with older children and adults, in neonates lung volume and functional residual capacity (FRC) as a percentage of body size are much less. Alveolar ventilation per unit lung volume is very high, because the neonate’s metabolic rate is about twice that of an adult. Most of this alveolar ventilation is provided by a rapid respiratory rate of 35 to 40 breaths/min because tidal volume is limited due to the structure of the chest wall.

One consequence of the reduced FRC and high metabolic rate in a neonate is a diminished reserve. Changes in the fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2) are rapidly seen as changes in the partial pressure of oxygen (PaO2), and the neonate quickly desaturates if ventilation is interrupted. This situation limits time for intubation, and airway management can be challenging. The high alveolar ventilation also accounts for a very rapid uptake of inhalational anesthetic agents, especially in premature infants, making it easy to overdose with these agents. Closing volume, which is the lung volume at which smaller airways tend to collapse, is very close to FRC in neonates. It is well known that anesthesia causes decreases in FRC. In a neonate, this low closing volume can result in airway closure at end expiration, with resultant atelectasis, ventilation/perfusion mismatch, and increased intrapulmonary shunting.

An awake infant uses laryngeal braking, resulting in an auto-positive end-expiratory pressure (auto-PEEP) to maintain FRC, but laryngeal braking is diminished by anesthesia. In a premature neonate, alveoli are immature, thick walled, and saccular. Surfactant production begins at 23 to 24 weeks’ gestation, but it may remain inadequate until 36 weeks’ gestational age; because of this, lung volumes and compliance are decreased further in very premature infants. Although the lung is less compliant in an infant than in an older child, the chest wall in an infant is very compliant. This combination results in increased work of breathing. Because resistance to airflow is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the radius of the airway, the work of breathing is increased further in neonates, particularly small premature infants.

Changes in airway resistance are also common during anesthesia, often resulting from small endotracheal tubes and equipment factors such as inspiratory and expiratory valves in the breathing circuit. Kinking of the endotracheal tube or the presence of secretions also can adversely affect resistance. Respiratory failure from fatigue can occur easily. Most anesthetic agents are respiratory depressants. Central regulation of breathing is obtunded under anesthesia, with a significant decrease in the ventilatory response to increased CO2. Most neonates require controlled positive-pressure ventilation during operative procedures because of the low FRC, increased closing volume, and increased work, along with changes induced by anesthetics. Infants already being ventilated require some increase in their ventilator settings after induction of anesthesia as spontaneous respiratory

Tracheomalacia is common in premature infants and, if low in the airway, may not be obviated by intubation. Bronchomalacia may result in airway collapse on expiration. Laryngomalacia is also common in premature infants and can result in obstruction with sedation prior to securing the airway. Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) or PEEP increases FRC and decreases closing volume and helps to stent open the airway during anesthesia. Slower respiratory rates should be used with positive-pressure ventilation to allow time for passive exhalation and prevent air trapping. Pneumothorax and interstitial emphysema may develop if high peak inspiratory pressures are used. Careful attention must be paid to ventilator settings, and one should anticipate changes that may need to occur during a surgical procedure.

Periodic breathing with intermittent apneic spells is common in neonates up to 3 months of age. Small premature infants have a biphasic ventilatory response to hypoxia, with an initial increase in ventilation, followed by a progressive decrease and eventual apnea. The ventilatory response to CO2 is decreased in premature infants and, as noted, is decreased further by anesthesia. Postoperative apneic spells are common in premature infants, although incidence decreases with advancing postconceptional age (PCA). These episodes can be secondary to the immature respiratory control system (central), a floppy airway (obstructive), or both (mixed or combined). Cote and coworkers25 did a meta-analysis of data from eight separate studies, and it was clear that the risk of apnea was strongly inversely related to gestational age and PCA. A full-term neonate is unlikely to experience significant postoperative apnea after 45 weeks’ PCA, whereas an infant born prematurely is at risk for postoperative apnea until 55 to 60 weeks’ PCA.25 The risk of postoperative apnea is increased in neonates who are anemic, suffer from neurologic disease, or are still currently experiencing apneic episodes. It is for these reasons that neonates coming in from home for surgical procedures are kept for a 12- to 24-hour period of respiratory monitoring until they are greater than 45 weeks’ PCA (full-term infants) or 55 to 60 weeks’ PCA (preterm infants).

### Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia and Oxygen Therapy

BPD is one of the most common complications of prematurity and can range from mild oxygen requirement to severe forms requiring prolonged mechanical ventilation with the development of pulmonary hypertension. The risk of BPD increases with decreasing gestational age at birth, as well as a number of other risk factors present at or shortly after birth.

Mechanical ventilation increases the risk of damage to the alveoli; however, mechanical ventilation is almost always

necessary intraoperatively with neonates. Especially in patients with severe BPD, low lung compliance at baseline makes invasive ventilation necessary in order to adequately oxygenate and ventilate while under the influence of anesthetic drugs as well as the potential need for muscle relaxation. In an attempt to avoid volutrauma and barotrauma, smaller tidal volumes should be employed with tolerance for mild hypercapnia (partial pressure of carbon dioxide in arterial blood [PaCO2], 55–60 mm Hg) assuming that pH is normal.23 Careful attention should be paid to the volume of intravenous fluids administered to avoid fluid overload and pulmonary edema, which can cause further lung damage.

Oxygen is a highly reactive molecule, and free-radical formation by oxygen is well known. Reperfusion injury, which refers to damage resulting from free-radical formation on oxygenation after a period of hypoxia, is well established. Retinopathy of prematurity is the most widely known complication of hyperoxia, but there is increasing evidence that oxygen may play a role in chronic lung disease, neurologic impairment, and other pathologic conditions. There is also evidence that wide fluctuations in oxygenation, as often experienced during anesthesia, may be damaging.

Monitoring of oxygenation during operative procedures is problematic. Continuous pulse oximetry is the standard of care and has contributed to the safety of anesthesia by avoidance of hypoxia. The pulse oximeter is not as helpful for the detection of hyperoxia. At hemoglobin saturations greater than 95%, most infants are hyperoxic; this is altered further by varying amounts of fetal hemoglobin. It has been suggested that for ongoing management of neonates in the NICU, oxygen saturation targets of 90% to 95% should be used.26 During the induction of anesthesia, brief increases in FiO2 are often necessary to allow for greater oxygen reserve while apneic during intubation; however, oxygen concentrations should be decreased quickly after the airway is secured. The presence of experienced personnel during intubation reduces the risk of prolonged apnea and desaturation during intubation. Intraoperatively, higher than normal oxygen concentrations may become necessary at times due to surgical techniques that may affect gas exchange (lung retraction, insufflation during laparoscopy, lateral decubitus positioning). Care must be taken to be cognizant of inspired oxygen concentrations, keeping them at the lowest concentration to maintain appropriate saturations whenever possible. Current anesthesia practice involves minimizing excessive oxygen administration in preterm neonates as long as oxygen saturation is 90% or greater.

### Airway Anatomy

Airway anatomy in neonates and infants differs from that of older children and must be taken into consideration when airway management is anticipated. The infant’s head is much larger relative to its body size, with a more prominent occiput and shorter neck than those of older children. The infant’s tongue is large, but the larynx is higher and anterior, with the cords located at C4 in the infant

The neonate’s larynx has historically been described as conical, with the narrowest point in the subglottic area at the cricoid ring. Studies have revisited this anatomy using MRI27 and video-bronchoscopic imaging.28 Based on these studies, the larynx is cylindrical, although not round in cross-section but rather elliptical, with the anteroposterior dimension slightly greater. A tight-fitting, round endotracheal tube might compress the lateral laryngeal mucosa; subglottic stenosis remains a concern, especially with longer term intubation. Current practice in pediatric anesthesia utilizes cuffed endotracheal tubes for most pediatric patients when intubating for surgical procedures.29 Changes in respiratory mechanics can occur as a result of surgical technique (laparoscopy, thoracoscopy, large abdominal incision with retraction). A cuffed endotracheal tube allows for changes in tidal volumes or inspiratory pressures with fewer leaks as lung compliance changes throughout the case.30 The endotracheal tube also protects the airway from aspiration of gastric contents or blood present due to surgical manipulation. There are robust safety data regarding the use of cuffed endotracheal tubes, even long term, in patients greater than 3 kg. Newer tubes with thin, low-pressure cuffs have allowed for the safe use of cuffed endotracheal tubes. Microcuff tubes are available with very thin cuffs and without the Murphy eye, which decreases the length of the tube below the cuff. This ensures that the entirety of the cuff is below the cords, avoiding pressure on the cords. A cuffed tube can be sized smaller, because the cuff prevents leakage and could decrease the incidence of subglottic stenosis rather than increase it, as previously believed, especially when attention is paid to cuff pressures. For patients less than 3 kg, little to no data are available regarding the use of cuffed endotracheal tubes as cuffed endotracheal tubes are only available down to 3.0-mm internal diameter.

Laryngeal and tracheal trauma is important because even modest airway edema can be serious. At the cricoid ring, 1 mm of edema results in a 60% reduction in the cross-sectional area of the airway, causing increased airway resistance and increased work of breathing.

### Cardiac Physiology

Immediately after birth, with an open ductus arteriosus, most of the cardiac output is from the left ventricle, and left ventricular end-diastolic volume is very high. Consequently, the neonatal heart functions at the high end of the Starling curve. As PVR decreases, output from the two ventricles becomes balanced at 150 to 200 mL/kg/min. Heart rate is rapid at 130 to 160 beats/min. Because end-diastolic volumes are already high, the infant heart is unable to increase stroke volume to a significant degree, and increases in cardiac output depend entirely on increases in heart rate. Baseline blood pressure is lower in infants than in older children, particularly in preterm infants, because cardiac output is increased due to a low SVR.

Almost all anesthetic agents have significant effects on the cardiovascular system. Inhalational agents tend to be cardiovascular depressants, and they can result in decreased myocardial contractility and subsequent decreased cardiac output. Most anesthetic agents cause decreased autonomic tone and peripheral vasodilation, decreasing afterload and preload. Because baroreceptor reflexes also are blunted by anesthesia, these decreases may make it impossible for the infant to compensate for pre-existing volume contraction or volume losses during anesthesia. Inotropic support may be necessary in a sick neonate, and almost all infants require some degree of volume loading during anesthesia to support tissue perfusion, urine output, and metabolic needs in the setting of anesthetic effects on hemodynamics.

### Fetal Hemoglobin and Anemia

The infant has approximately 80% fetal hemoglobin (hemoglobin F) at birth. Hemoglobin F has a P50 (PaO2 at which hemoglobin is 50% saturated) of 20 mm Hg compared with a P50 of 27 mm Hg for hemoglobin A, which means that hemoglobin F has a higher affinity for oxygen and that the hemoglobin dissociation curve is shifted to the left. In utero, this hemoglobin dissociation curve favors transport of oxygen from the maternal to the fetal circulation. Put another way, for any given oxygen saturation, the infant has a lower PaO2. Unloading of oxygen at the tissue level also is diminished, although this is compensated for by an increased hemoglobin level of approximately 17.5 g/dL at birth. The decreased unloading can result in tissue hypoxia, however, if PaO2, hemoglobin, or cardiac output decreases during surgery, with secondary development of metabolic acidosis. The hemoglobin increases slightly just after birth, then decreases progressively to a level of 9.5 to 11 g/dL by 7 to 9 weeks of life due to reduced red blood cell life span, increasing blood volume, and immature hematopoiesis. Hemoglobin F synthesis begins to decrease after 35 weeks’ gestation, and hemoglobin F is completely replaced by hemoglobin A by 8 to 12 weeks of life, paralleling the decrease in hemoglobin and helping to maintain tissue oxygenation. The physiologic hemoglobin nadir may occur earlier and may be more pronounced in premature infants, as they have impaired erythropoietin production as well as potential blood losses from frequent phlebotomy and reduced red blood cell life span. These factors place them at higher risk for anemia of prematurity. Preoperative anemia in neonates has been found to be an independent risk factor for mortality after noncardiac surgery.31 When these patients present for surgical procedures requiring anesthesia, an otherwise well-tolerated physiologic anemia may necessitate transfusion in the operating room to optimize tissue oxygenation, replacing even small amounts of blood loss. Anemia is also a risk factor for postoperative apnea, which may have an effect on the ability to successfully extubate a premature neonate after an anesthetic. It is for these reasons that preoperative red blood cell transfusions with a hemoblobin goal of at least 10 g/dL is indicated in anemic neonates.

### Renal Physiology

Nephrogenesis is complete at 34 weeks’ gestation, and the term neonate has as many nephrons as an adult, although they are immature, with a glomerular filtration rate (GFR) approximately 30% of the adult GFR. With increasing cardiac output and decreasing renal vascular resistance, renal blood flow and GFR increase rapidly over the first few weeks of life and reach adult levels by about 1 year of life. The diminished function over the first year is well balanced to the infant’s needs, because much of the neonate’s solute load is incorporated into body growth, and the excretory load is smaller.

Several aspects of renal physiology are pertinent to anesthesia care. First, the neonatal kidney has only limited concentrating ability, whereas antidiuretic hormone secretion and activity are normal. Coupled with an increased insensible loss due to a “thin” skin and increased ratio of surface area to volume, the limited concentrating ability of the kidney implies a tendency to become water depleted if intake or administration is inadequate. The neonatal kidney also is unable to excrete dilute urine efficiently and cannot handle a large free water load. In addition, primarily due to a short, immature proximal tubule, infants are obligate sodium wasters. There is a tendency toward hyponatremia, especially if too much free water is administered during surgery, which can easily happen with continuous infusions from invasive pressure transducers or fluid boluses. Because of the lower GFR, the neonate also cannot handle a large sodium load and can easily develop volume overload and congestive heart failure. With the frequent need for volume or blood product administration in the operative setting, consideration of immature renal physiology must occur.

One final aspect of concern is acid-base status: The neonatal kidney wastes small amounts of bicarbonate due to an immature proximal tubule; infants are born with a mild proximal renal tubular acidosis, with serum bicarbonate of approximately 20 mmol/L. All of these changes are greater in preterm infants, particularly before nephrogenesis is complete at 34 weeks.

### Temperature Regulation

Given a large surface area, small body volume, and minimal insulation, neonates are extremely prone to heat loss. Any degree of cold stress is detrimental and increases metabolic demands in the neonate. Infants are unable to shiver effectively, and cold stress causes catecholamine release, which stimulates nonshivering thermogenesis by brown fat. Premature infants have less brown fat, decreasing their capacity for nonshivering thermogenesis and increasing their risk for hypothermia. The increased catechols caused by cold stress can be detrimental, causing increased peripheral vascular resistance and SVR, increased cardiac stress, and increased oxygen consumption. Anesthesia blunts thermoregulatory sensitivity and interferes with nonshivering thermogenesis and brown fat metabolism. Anesthesia also increases heat loss

by inducing cutaneous vasodilation. Surgical factors such as major operations with open body cavities also contribute to increased risks of hypothermia in the neonate. Hypothermia can result in increased metabolic oxygen demand, respiratory depression, bradycardia, coagulopathy, and impaired wound healing. At all times, including during transport and in the operating room, the infant must be subjected to a neutral thermal environment. An environment that is too warm can be equally detrimental. Core temperature must be carefully monitored at all times in the operating room. Higher than normal ambient operating room temperatures, forced air warmers, overhead radiant warmers, warming of fluids and blood products prior to administration, and minimizing exposure (such as wearing hats) are methods to help maintain euthermia during surgery.

### Carbohydrate Metabolism

Whole-body glucose demand corrected for body mass in neonates can be twice that in adults. Carbohydrate reserves, primarily hepatic glycogen, in a normal newborn are relatively low, and even lower in an infant with low birth weight. Hypoglycemia can readily occur if the infant is deprived of a glucose source. Under anesthesia, the symptoms of hypoglycemia (jitteriness, altered level of consciousness, apnea, tachypnea, poor feeding) are masked, so careful monitoring of serum glucose is indicated for procedures lasting longer than 2 to 3 hours so that low serum glucose levels are not missed. Even transient hypoglycemia may be associated with neurologic injury and developmental delay in neonates.32 Generally, intravenous glucose or intravenous hyperalimentation should be continued during periods of preoperative fasting and intraoperatively, especially in infants with low birth weight without adequate glycogen or fat stores. In contrast with adults in whom hyperglycemia seems to potentiate brain damage during global and focal ischemia, hyperglycemia in neonates may provide some protection from ischemic damage.58 Nonetheless, hyperglycemia can also be a problem in the perioperative period. Insulin response is deficient in preterm infants, and high catecholamines due to illness or intraoperative stress can result in hyperglycemia.

### Transport of the Neonate

Transport of a premature infant may be as great a risk as the surgery itself. Dedicated transport incubators, with a built-in ventilator, air and oxygen supplies, and a blender should be used if possible. In addition to the inherent risks involved in the transport of a potentially unstable patient, premature neonates are particularly susceptible to cold stress. Heat loss during transport must be addressed because the hospital corridors are rarely neutral thermal environments. If the infant is in an incubator, the incubator should be used for transport, because heat is retained even when it is unplugged. An infant on an open radiant warmer should be covered, including the head. In some institutions, plastic

The use of a simple oxygen tank limits ventilation to 100% FiO2, so controlled oxygen delivery requires an additional air tank and a blender. The anesthesia bag always should include a manometer, because it is easy to reach pressures that can result in barotrauma complications such as pneumothorax. A self-inflating resuscitator can be used for room-air ventilation, and a PEEP valve can be added to the device. In an intubated infant, CPAP or PEEP can be maintained using devices such as the Neopuff. Any pumps providing infusions to the infant should have adequate battery power to operate throughout the transport, especially if vasoactive drips are running. Syringe pumps provide a very stable rate and have a long battery life, and the entire system is compact, minimizing the equipment needing transport. These pumps also run accurately at a low (0.5 mL/h) rate so that concentrated infusions can be used, minimizing fluid delivered to the neonate.

A complete round of resuscitative medications also should accompany any infant being transported to or from the NICU. Transports often require multiple personnel— anesthesia staff, nursing, and respiratory therapy. With

planning and adequate personnel, the transport of infants on extracorporeal membrane oxygenation or infants receiving inhaled nitric oxide is possible.

In some situations, if the surgical procedure is appropriate, the surgeon is amenable, and a suitable location is available, it may be preferable to perform some procedures in the NICU. Basic requirements for a suitable locale include a clean area that can be closed off from traffic and adequate equipment, including overhead lights, surgical instruments and supplies, appropriate monitors, and anesthesia equipment. For premature neonates, an anesthesia machine is not usually needed, and a standard neonatal ventilator can be used. In many state-of-the-art NICUs, there is a dedicated operating room, with appropriate equipment, gases, and lights within the NICU, so that the most critically ill infants can be cared for with minimal transport.

### Operating Room Equipment and Monitoring

The operating room should not merely replicate NICU capabilities; it should surpass them, because the neonate is subjected to the additional stress and destabilization of surgery. It is helpful if the room itself has adequate temperature control, because it may be necessary to increase room temperature to obtain a neutral thermal environment. Before draping, radiant heat lamps can be used, although care must be taken not to place the lamps too close to the infant because overheating can occur. The operating tables for neonates should use a heating pad. For longer cases, forcedair heaters with a “full access” disposable air blanket that is placed under the infant may be used. Care does have to be taken that the sheets and drapes around the infant are dry, however, as evaporative cooling can occur with the continuous air flow if the child is wet. Maintenance fluids, because they are given at a relatively slow rate, usually can be given at room temperature, but fluid warmers must be available for blood or faster fluid administration. Cooling is rarely necessary, but it is possible to overheat an infant if care is not taken. Temperature must be monitored. Core temperature should be measured whenever possible. It can be measured with a rectal, nasopharyngeal, or esophageal probe. Bladder and tympanic membrane probes are rarely used in neonates because of size. Skin temperature is a poor choice for monitoring temperature, as it often better approximates the environmental temperature rather than the core temperature in a small infant.

Routine monitoring requirements for neonates are listed in Box 39.1. Continuous pulse oximetry has revolutionized anesthesia, and it is a standard of care in neonates as in adults. In some situations, particularly with congenital heart disease or PPHN, two pulse oximeters may be used to monitor preductal and postductal oxygen saturations. Heart rate is monitored from the pulse oximeter and the ECG. Disposable neonatal ECG pads are needed, from a size standard and because they may adhere better to the vernix-covered skin of the neonate. With a typical capnograph, the accuracy depends on the actual site of sampling, the type of anesthesia circuit used, and the volume of fresh gas flow through the circuit. The most accurate measurements are obtained using a low dead space circuit, with the sampling site in the endotracheal tube, not on the circuit. Dead spaces within the anesthesia circuit or due to the addition of capnography samplers into a neonatal

Transcutaneous CO2 monitoring is used with increased frequency in the NICU but is not used routinely in the operating room.

Cerebral oximetry employing near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) can provide information on changes in cerebral blood flow and can provide real-time measurement of cerebral tissue oxygenation. In neonatal patients where invasive arterial monitoring can be challenging and lower limits of acceptable blood pressure in anesthetized neonates are unknown, the ability to detect changes in cerebral tissue oxygenation in these vulnerable patients can provide helpful information. NIRS monitoring is used routinely in pediatric cardiac surgery, pediatric intensive care units (PICUs), and NICUs, but we do not have sufficient data to determine if large-scale use of NIRS monitoring in neonates under anesthesia can have an effect on neurodevelopmental outcome.35 Previously, many anesthesia machines were equipped with a rudimentary, volume-limited, time-cycled ventilator, which even with a pediatric bellows was poorly suited for neonatal ventilation. Small tidal volumes were very difficult to set, and tidal volume and pressure varied tremendously depending on the fresh gas flow. In the best of hands, these ventilators are impossible to use with premature neonates. Newer anesthesia machines incorporate significantly more sophisticated ventilators, capable of either volume-limited or pressure-limited ventilation. These ventilators can be used in pressure-limited, time-cycled mode, and they incorporate a spirometer that can measure expired tidal volumes as small as10 mL. Fresh gas flow is uncoupled from tidal volume, and changes in flows do not affect ventilation. PEEP can easily be added without the external valves used in older machines. These machines can be used routinely in infants weighing as little as 1000 g.

An alternative method is to bring a NICU ventilator to the operating room. Critically ill neonates with high ventilator settings may be best served by the accuracy of a NICU ventilator. Using a neonatal ventilator does prevent the use of inhalational anesthetic agents that can only be delivered from an anesthesia machine, so a total intravenous anesthetic technique is necessary.

The circle breathing system, with inspiratory and expiratory valves and incorporating a CO2 absorber, has become standard in adult anesthesia. A major advantage is that a semi-closed technique with very low gas flows can be used, conserving anesthetic agent. Similar circle systems, appropriately sized for infants with lower compliance tubing and smaller bags, are commonly used in neonates.

### General Anesthesia for the Neonate

Most infants who require surgery receive a general anesthetic. There is increasing interest in regional techniques, but most often this is still combined with a general anesthetic in order to provide for a still surgical field. Successful delivery of general anesthesia in neonates requires knowledge of developmental pharmacology to predict and understand the responses of premature infants to anesthetic drugs. Size has an effect on response to anesthetics, and developmental age has a profound impact on the dose-response, distribution, and metabolism of these drugs.

### Inhalational Agents

Inhalational anesthetics agents include the halogenated volatile anesthetics (sevoflurane, isoflurane, and desflurane) and nitrous oxide. These potent anesthetic gases are delivered via vaporizers into specialized airway circuits connected to anesthesia machines. When delivered into the lungs, these gases are taken up into the bloodstream in order to reach the central nervous system, where they exert their effects.

Careful administration of inhaled anesthetics can allow for safe use of these drugs during the maintenance phase of anesthesia. The anesthetic effect of inhalational agents depends on the partial pressure of the anesthetic in the brain and the potency of the agent. For several reasons, very high partial pressures of the inhalational agents in the brain develop much more rapidly in neonates than in older children and adults. First, as already discussed, the ratio of alveolar ventilation (per minute) to FRC in neonates is 5:1 compared with 1.5:1 in adults; consequently, alveolar anesthetic concentration equilibrates with inspired concentration very quickly. Second, a greater fraction of the cardiac

output in the neonate is distributed to the vessel-rich group and consequently the brain. Finally, the solubility of the inhaled anesthetics in blood is less in neonates than in adults.

Sevoflurane and isoflurane are most commonly used in neonates. Volatile anesthetics are complete anesthetics, with analgesic and amnesic properties. SVR is decreased by isoflurane and hypotension can result, especially if preload is diminished. Moderate volume loading helps to minimize any decrease in blood pressure. Isoflurane also causes cerebral vasodilation, and, in the absence of hypotension, cerebral blood flow increases. In adults, isoflurane decreases cerebral metabolism and is cerebral protective.

Sevoflurane has become very popular in pediatric anesthesia due to its usefulness for inhalation induction. It is not irritating to the airway, and it is almost insoluble in blood so that equilibration between brain and alveolus occurs rapidly. Onset of anesthesia during mask induction is very fast and may be used for mask induction in healthier neonates. Cardiovascular effects are similar to effects with isoflurane. Sevoflurane has been associated with prolongation of the Q-T interval of the ECG in adults and infants.

In the neonate, inhaled anesthetics are most commonly used during the maintenance phase of anesthesia after intravenous anesthetics are used for the induction phase. Rarely, if a neonate presents to the operating room without intravenous access, the inhalation agent sevoflurane can be administered in higher concentrations to perform an inhalation induction of anesthesia. Isoflurane is very pungent and cannot be used for mask induction. Higher doses of volatile anesthetics required for an inhalation induction may be poorly tolerated, causing hypotension, bradycardia, and decreased cardiac output. Brain tissue equilibrates very quickly with the alveolar concentration of anesthetic, increasing the risk of overdose in a neonate.

The potency of inhalational anesthetics is expressed using the minimum alveolar concentration (MAC). The MAC is the concentration at which 50% of patients exhibit no response to surgical stimulation such as skin incision. The MAC is related to PCA and is lowest in very premature neonates, increasing to a peak at a PCA of approximately 1 year and then decreasing progressively from childhood through adulthood. Fig. 39.2 shows this relationship for isoflurane.36 Isoflurane is more potent (lower MAC) in premature neonates than in older infants.

Nitrous oxide is an inhalational anesthetic, but it is not in the same class as the halogenated agents. It is a weak anesthetic, with a MAC of 104% in adults; in order to reach MAC, nitrous oxide would have to be provided at hyperbaric pressures in addition to utilizing hypoxic mixtures of gas. The need for oxygen as part of inspired gases prevents achievement of these levels. Nitrous oxide is almost insoluble, and the onset of effect is fast. These properties cause nitrous oxide to progressively enter and expand any gasfilled space in contact with the circulation, which rapidly leads to bowel distention or expansion of pneumothorax. If ventilation is interrupted for any reason, nitrous oxide

### Intravenous Agents

Intravenous anesthetic agents for use in neonates include propofol, ketamine, opioids, and benzodiazepines. Propofol is a phenol derivative supplied as an emulsion in lipid, which is used for induction and maintenance of anesthesia. Recovery from the drug is rapid due to redistribution and metabolism by liver and tissues. Propofol has few analgesic effects, and for painful operations it should be used with additional analgesics. Propofol has been approved for children over 2 months of age, but great care must be taken when administering it due to significant interindividual variability, especially at extremes of age. Larger initial doses (2–3 mg/kg) are often necessary in neonates due to a larger volume of extracellular fluid, but they exhibit a slower recovery due to less fat and muscle for redistribution, as well as slower hepatic metabolism due to immaturity. When used as an infusion, dosing should be decreased in neonates to account for slower clearance.37 It is a potent peripheral vasodilator, and significant protracted hypotension after bolus dosing is a common problem limiting its use in preterm neonates.38

Ketamine is a phencyclidine derivative that acts as an N-methyl-d-aspartate (NMDA) receptor antagonist; it provides good hypnosis and amnesia and excellent analgesia. When used as a sole agent in adults and older children, it can cause a dissociative state with confusion, hallucinations, and other severe psychological side effects. Ketamine stimulates the sympathetic nervous system and causes minimal

respiratory and cardiovascular depression, which may make it a useful adjunct in the anesthetic care of the infant. Blood pressure may increase, and increased intracranial pressure is a concern in infants with hydrocephalus or those at risk for intraventricular hemorrhage. Ketamine can be useful in breaking hypercyanotic spells caused by increased right-toleft shunting in infants with tetralogy of Fallot, because it anesthetizes and increases SVR.

Benzodiazepines are agents that produce sedation, anxiolysis, and amnesia, but little analgesia. They are incomplete anesthetic agents, although in adults they have been very useful in combination with an opioid. Midazolam is a very short-acting benzodiazepine, and it has been the most commonly used in anesthesia. Metabolism is almost entirely hepatic, and it should be expected that duration would be prolonged by immature hepatic function in a preterm neonate. Midazolam causes vasodilation, which can result in hypotension. In high doses, it can cause respiratory depression, although this is more common in conjunction with opioids. Midazolam and the longer-acting benzodiazepine lorazepam have been used for sedation in the NICU with mixed results. The Cochrane Neonatal Collaborative Review Group performed a meta-analysis of several studies on sedation in the NICU using midazolam. All three studies showed that midazolam was effective at providing sedation to the neonate. However, one study showed a higher risk of poor neurologic outcome or death in the midazolam-treated group, as well as evidence of increased length of stay, which at least raises questions as to the safety of midazolam infusion in these infants.39

Morphine is the principal opium alkaloid, and it is the standard against which analgesics are measured. Morphine is less potent than fentanyl, but it has a longer duration of action and is more commonly used for postoperative pain. Due to immature hepatic metabolism, the duration of action of morphine is increased in premature infants which should be taken into account when determining the frequency of intermittent boluses. As with all opioids, respiratory depression is a major side effect. In contrast to fentanyl, morphine causes histamine release, which limits the ability to use it in high doses as an anesthetic agent, although it is well accepted for analgesia, postoperative pain, and overall sedation. Morphine distribution in neonates has been well studied and is very predictable, although required target concentrations in neonates are still uncertain.

Fentanyl, a synthetic opioid, is widely used in neonatal anesthesia, and it is the most commonly used anesthetic for premature infants. It has a wide safety margin and beneficial effects on hemodynamic stability. Fentanyl can block pulmonary hypertensive crises, and it is useful in infants with pulmonary hypertension, such as infants with congenital diaphragmatic hernia, PPHN, and some cardiac defects. The pharmacokinetics of fentanyl in the early neonatal period is widely variable, depending on gestational and postnatal age and the type of surgery and medical comorbidities of the infant. Fentanyl is primarily metabolized in the liver, with only a small amount excreted unchanged by the kidneys.

Clearance is lowest in the most premature infants, and it increases with gestational age and with age after birth, probably reflecting increasing hepatic maturation. Volume of distribution of fentanyl also seems to vary depending on gestational age and disease state. Neonates with increased intra-abdominal pressure seem to have slower clearance of fentanyl, likely due to the resulting decreased hepatic blood flow.

Given the highly variable pharmacodynamics, fentanyl dosing should start low (0.25 μg/kg) and be titrated to clinical effect. There is a fairly wide therapeutic range, and even with high doses, hemodynamic stability is maintained. All narcotics are respiratory depressants, however, and with higher doses of fentanyl, prolonged respiratory depression occurs, necessitating postoperative assisted ventilation.

Fentanyl in combination with a muscle relaxant has become the standard for anesthesia in very premature neonates. This combination may also be used during elective (nonemergent) intubation in the NICU. Although fentanyl is a potent analgesic, it is not a complete anesthetic, and occasionally in adults, awareness has occurred with high-dose fentanyl alone. In the past, it was suggested that this was of minimal importance because neonates are not “aware,” especially if pain was adequately treated. This belief is less well accepted today, and benzodiazepines or inhalational agents such as isoflurane are more commonly added to fentanyl anesthesia in the operating room.

Other synthetic narcotics such as alfentanil and sufentanil rarely have been used in neonates. In adults, alfentanil is less potent than fentanyl, but it has a shorter half-life, whereas sufentanil is more potent than fentanyl. The pharmacokinetics in infants is probably similar to fentanyl, and there does not seem to be any significant advantage compared with fentanyl. Remifentanil is a newer opioid whose duration of action is terminated by hydrolysis by tissue esterases. Consequently, remifentanil does not accumulate or have prolonged duration of action. A half-life of 4.4 minutes and a clearance of 80 mL/kg/min have been reported in neonates.40 Duration of action is very short, and it may be of use for procedural analgesia with little persistent pain. Duration can be extended by using a continuous infusion, but this can be associated with opioid-induced tolerance and hyperalgesia.40,41

Acetaminophen is one of the most commonly used analgesic medications for neonates. Acetaminophen is considered to be a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID), and it exerts its analgesic effects via inhibition of cyclooxygenase enzymes and decreasing prostaglandin synthesis. It has frequently been used as an adjunct for pain relief postoperatively, and its use after major abdominal or thoracic procedures is associated with a decrease in opioid consumption.42 Previously, the use of acetaminophen intraoperatively was limited to the rectal route of administration which is known to have variable uptake and effectiveness. However, the availability of an intravenous formulation has allowed for the routine use of acetaminophen intraoperatively as an adjunct analgesic. Dosing should be adjusted based on PCA

(7.5–10 mg/kg for patients <36 weeks’ PCA) to avoid the risk of hepatic toxicity, as clearance of the drug is lower.43

Dexmedetomidine is a highly specific alpha2-adrenergic agonist with hypnotic, analgesic, and anxiolytic properties. It is being used with increased frequency in the pediatric setting for sedation during nonpainful procedures such as MRI, as an adjunct to other anesthetics during surgical procedures, and for sedation of critically ill patients in the ICU setting. Despite the sedating properties of dexmedetomidine, there is little effect on respiratory function, thereby promoting earlier extubation and decreasing the need for analgesics that have respiratory depressant properties. Numerous studies have demonstrated the effectiveness and safety of dexmedetomidine as an analgesic and sedative in infants after cardiac surgery. Adverse effects of dexmedetomidine include bradycardia and hypotension, as well as paradoxical hypertension, but it has been found to be well tolerated in neonates.44 The drug undergoes hepatic metabolism and therefore has decreased plasma clearance and a longer elimination half-life in preterm neonates with immature hepatocyte function.45 Preliminary data in animal studies show evidence that dexmedetomidine may actually protect against neuroapoptosis caused by other anesthetic agents.46

### Neuromuscular Blocking Agents

Muscle relaxants are commonly used in anesthesia for neonates. They are often grouped according to mechanism of action (i.e., depolarizing vs. nondepolarizing), but it is more important to consider rapidity of onset and duration of action. Succinylcholine is the only depolarizing agent used at present, and it remains the standard for rapid onset and rapid disappearance. The ED95 (effective dose in 95% of the population receiving the dose) in neonates for succinylcholine is at least twice that of adults at 2 to 3 mg/ kg. Action is terminated by metabolism by plasma pseudocholinesterase. Succinylcholine is not routinely used in children because of several rare but serious adverse reactions. In patients with myopathies or neurologic diseases, succinylcholine can cause overwhelming hyperkalemia, muscle necrosis, and cardiac arrest that is refractory to resuscitation. Bradycardia also occasionally occurs during intubation in infants with succinylcholine. For this reason, some anesthesiologists routinely administer atropine with succinylcholine. In pediatric patients, succinylcholine is reserved primarily for rapid sequence induction when a full stomach is suspected.

Nondepolarizing relaxants competitively inhibit acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction. Vecuronium bromide is an intermediate-acting relaxant occasionally used in neonates. It has little effect on the cardiac system, although it may cause bradycardia in combination with narcotics. Cisatracurium besylate undergoes spontaneous degradation by a chemical process (Hofmann elimination), and duration is not affected by liver or kidney function. Rocuronium bromide is an agent with a rapid onset of action that can be used in place of succinylcholine for rapid sequence

Most relaxants probably have a prolonged duration of action in premature neonates, and frequency of dosing should be determined using a nerve stimulator to measure response to four spaced stimuli (train-of-four response). This type of monitoring can be challenging with small premature neonates. At the completion of surgery, muscle relaxation with nondepolarizing agents should be reversed. An anticholinesterase, typically neostigmine, and an anticholinergic, such as glycopyrrolate or atropine, can be used for reversal. Sugammadex, a newer reversal agent for the commonly used muscle relaxants rocuronium and vecuronium, is currently approved as a reversal agent in children over 2 years old. However, there are a number of cases series of sugammadex being used “off-label” in neonates and infants without significant adverse events.47 Sugammadex has the benefit of being able to reverse profound neuromuscular blockade (unlike neostigmine), but further studies are needed to confirm its safety in neonates.

### Induction of General Anesthesia

Most sick infants have intravenous access, and an intravenous induction can be performed. Premedication rarely is given to neonates, although some anesthesiologists recommend glycopyrrolate or atropine before laryngoscopy and intubation to mitigate any possible vagal response and bradycardia with intubation. Healthier infants without intravenous access can undergo mask induction, typically with 50% nitrous oxide and sevoflurane, after which intravenous access is rapidly obtained.

Infants with a full stomach, most commonly infants with intra-abdominal disease, must have an intravenous rapidsequence induction. During rapid-sequence induction, the infant is first preoxygenated with 100% FiO2 to maximize oxygenation during the apneic period of intubation. An intravenous induction agent such as propofol, along with a fast-acting paralytic, is administered in rapid succession. The use of cricoid pressure to prevent regurgitation of gastric contents is not routinely considered, as it can actually hinder successful intubation by obscuring the view of the glottic opening during laryngoscopy.48 Positive-pressure ventilation is avoided or provided very gently, and the infant is intubated expertly as soon as conditions are appropriate, usually after 45 to 90 seconds. There is little room for error with rapid sequence induction, and it should be performed only by individuals with significant expertise.

Maintenance of spontaneous ventilation may be considered if there is significant concern for a difficult airway, such as in Pierre Robin and Goldenhar syndromes. Maintenance of spontaneous ventilation is beneficial during situations where mask ventilation may be difficult and time to successful intubation may be prolonged. When the airway is secured, muscle relaxation can be administered as necessary. In the past, awake intubations were often considered when a difficult airway was suspected in order to maintain spontaneous ventilation and airway reflexes. However,

awake intubations are now known to cause higher rates of airway trauma and can have significant hemodynamic consequences in the neonate such as arterial hypertension, pulmonary hypertensive crisis, and increased intracranial pressure due to pain and sympathetic stimulation.49 This technique is rarely used in the operating room.

When the potential for a difficult airway exists, careful planning is necessary to ensure the availability of specialty equipment, as well as the availability of additional “trained hands.” Intubation should occur in a controlled manner whenever possible, and elective intubation should be considered early to avoid emergency airway situations. A pediatric fiberoptic bronchoscope and a range of special-purpose laryngoscope blades may be useful. LMAs should be available to assist with ventilation, but they do not protect the airway from aspiration. The pediatric bronchoscope also can be used to intubate through the LMA. Video laryngoscopes may be helpful, especially in the setting of intubation by trainees. Pediatric ear, nose, and throat consultation may also be necessary for expertise in rigid bronchoscopy.

### Regional Anesthesia and Local Anesthetics

Concerns about the neurotoxicity of general anesthetic agents and widespread availability of ultrasound have resulted in increased interest in regional anesthesia in children and neonates. Ultrasound has made it both easier and safer to perform regional blocks in children. Regional anesthesia techniques include local infiltration, fascial plane blocks, peripheral nerve blocks, and neuraxial anesthesia. Regional techniques are commonly combined with general anesthesia, with the goals of reducing intraoperative anesthetic requirements, decreasing postoperative analgesic requirements, and promoting earlier extubation. Analysis of data from the Pediatric Regional Anesthesia Network (PRAN) comprised of more than 100,000 blocks demonstrated that the risk of major complications when performing regional anesthesia on anesthetized children is exceedingly rare, with no permanent neurologic deficits reported.50 This analysis included almost 10,000 regional anesthetics in neonates and infants. There are inherent technical difficulties to performing regional anesthesia in neonates, including the need for appropriate-sized catheters and the need for specialized training to perform these blocks safely and successfully. However, there are numerous reports of safe and effective administration of regional anesthesia in neonates.

Local infiltration or distal nerve block is useful in certain specific procedures such as circumcision, where a dorsal penile nerve block (DPNB) or penile ring block has been shown to be effective as a sole anesthetic. Other simple methods, such as a sucrose-dipped pacifier or a padded and physiologic restraint chair, further decrease objective signs of distress during circumcision performed with DPNB. A eutectic mixture of local anesthetic (EMLA) cream also has been used for neonatal circumcision. Other indications for use of EMLA include venous and arterial puncture,

Neuraxial regional anesthetic techniques include epidural and spinal anesthesia. Neuraxial anesthesia aims to make an area of the body insensate through the administration of local anesthetic into either the intrathecal or epidural space. In neonates and infants, the epidural space can be easily entered by the caudal route through the sacrococcygeal membrane (Fig. 39.3). Caudal anesthesia is a useful option for surgeries involving the lower abdomen, groin, and lower extremities. Caudal anesthesia given as a single injection is commonly used in combination with a general anesthetic to allow for lower concentrations of inhalational agents and provide postoperative pain control, but it can occasionally be used as the sole anesthetic. After a caudal anesthetic with bupivacaine or ropivacaine, most infants are free of pain immediately after surgery, with relief continuing for at least 4 hours. The single-shot technique utilizes a 22-gauge, short-bevel needle or 22-gauge angiocath to enter the caudal space. Caudal anesthesia requires a higher dosage of local anesthetic than a spinal anesthetic, so the possibility of an inadvertent intravascular injection is a concern.

A catheter can also be threaded via the caudal route up to the thoracic epidural space or it can be inserted and threaded directly into the thoracic or lumbar epidural space if continuous analgesia is needed for multiple days. Epidural catheters allow for the continuous infusion of local anesthetic intra- and postoperatively, thereby minimizing the need for analgesics that may result in respiratory depression or may have altered pharmacokinetic properties in the immature neonate. This technique is well tolerated without significant hemodynamic effect. Despite the ability to perform these procedures, there has long been concern over the safety of these techniques in the neonatal patient. An observational study utilizing the PRAN was able to evaluate the incidence of complications related to the use of neuraxial catheters in patients under 1 month of age. With over 300 neuraxial catheters placed, the most common complications were catheter malfunction, catheter contamination, and vascular aspiration, all of which were managed by removal or adjustment of the catheter. There were no reports of more serious complications, such as persistent neurologic injury, deep infection, or epidural hematoma.51

With the increased use of ultrasound for regional anesthesia, truncal or fascial plane blocks have been gaining popularity. The injection and spread of local anesthetic within a fascial plane targets nerves traveling within the plane and adjacent tissue. They are less invasive than neuraxial techniques and appear to be low risk, as local anesthetic is injected into a fascial plane, which avoids larger nerve bundles or the neuraxial space. These fascial plane blocks are relatively easy to perform in neonates compared to more challenging neuraxial techniques. Regional anesthesia in the pediatric patient is most commonly performed under general anesthesia with an exceedingly low complication rate.50 A regional technique without general anesthesia can be used in some neonates considered to be at high risk, such as those with severe BPD, in whom avoidance of intubation for a general anesthetic is preferred in addition to avoiding the potential negative effects of anesthesia on neurocognitive development.52 Despite the avoidance of a general anesthetic, the most robust study comparing general anesthesia to awake regional anesthesia did not reveal an overall reduction in postoperative apnea in those patients receiving a regional anesthetic, but the infants receiving spinal anesthesia had fewer clinically significant apneas.53 Spinal anesthesia can be performed using a 25-gauge Quincke needle at the L4 or L5 level (below the cauda equina). Due to the duration of the block, surgical procedures must be completed in less than 90 minutes in order for spinal anesthesia to be considered. Commonly used local anesthetics for regional anesthesia in neonates and infants include bupivacaine, ropivacaine, 2-chloroprocaine, and tetracaine. Careful attention must be paid to the dosing of local anesthetics, especially with the use of continuous epidural infusions, to avoid potentially toxic doses. Many local anesthetics are metabolized by hepatic enzymes that are immature in the neonate. These physiologic differences place neonates and infants at higher risk for local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST), as reduced clearance can result in local anesthetic accumulation. Maximum dosages of local anesthetics are reduced in neonates and infants to minimize the risk of toxicity. The use of 2-chloroprocaine for continuous infusions may reduce the risk of LAST, as it is metabolized by plasma cholinesterase, resulting in a much shorter half-life.55

### Maintenance of Anesthesia

Maintenance of anesthesia requires full monitoring throughout with, at a minimum, continuous ECG, pulse oximetry, and end-tidal CO2 as well as frequent noninvasive blood pressure monitoring. Temperature should also be monitored and must be carefully controlled with adjustments in heating or cooling as appropriate. Fluid and metabolic requirements also must be carefully assessed throughout the course of the surgery. Fluids should be administered with an infusion pump to prevent inadvertent fluid overload. It is usually easiest to calculate and administer maintenance fluids separately from replacement. Maintenance fluids should include glucose unless the infant is known to be hyperglycemic. Intravenous hyperalimentation or a dextrose-electrolyte solution can be used, depending on the size, age, and clinical condition of the neonate. Intraoperatively, glucose requirements are often lower than normal maintenance requirements, as surgical stress results in increased catecholamine and cortisol levels and decreased plasma insulin with resulting hyperglycemia. Care should be taken to avoid interruptions in glucose-containing infusions and to monitor blood glucose levels when surgical procedures exceed 2 to 3 hours. Third-space losses should be initially replaced with a balanced crystalloid solution such as lactated Ringer’s. Blood loss also can be replaced with crystalloid initially.

Third-space losses can be impressive, ranging from 2 to 15 mL/kg/h, especially during procedures with large amounts of bowel exposed, such as for repair of gastroschisis and omphalocele or bowel resection. Many infants, especially if they are hypoalbuminemic, should receive some replacement as colloids, usually 5% albumin. Transfusion with packed red blood cells, fresh frozen plasma, and platelets may be required. If significant surgical blood loss is anticipated, blood products should be prepared prior to the start of surgery in order to ensure that products can be appropriately prepared. Packed red blood cells should be washed, leukoreduced, and irradiated prior to transfusion. Blood products should be administered in small aliquots, ideally from a single donor if possible. Urine output should be followed as one sign of adequate fluid replacement.

Ventilation should be carefully controlled. Use of oxygen has been discussed; if controlled ventilation is employed, care should be taken to avoid hyperventilation and subsequent hypocapnia. Higher peak pressures can cause significant barotrauma. Accurate ventilation may be difficult to monitor because varying anesthesia circuits and adapters can result in widely varying dead space and a variable offset between end-tidal CO2 and the actual blood partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PCO2). Premature neonates, especially those less than 1500 g, often benefit from the use of an ICU ventilator for better accuracy of delivered volumes.

### Recovery From Anesthesia

Emergence from anesthesia in the smallest and sickest premature infants may be a prolonged event, and these neonates are not typical candidates for extubation at the conclusion of surgery; instead, they require continued intensive care in the NICU. Immaturity of drug clearance systems also prolongs recovery from the effects of most anesthetic agents in these infants. Older and healthier neonates, even those that are premature, can often be extubated after many types
